WRITE SIDE READ SIDE ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ PostCommandGateway (is the handler) │ │ PostQueryGateway (is the handler) │ │ impl CommandHandler<PublishPost> │ │ impl QueryHandler<FindPost> │ │ find │ decide │ ctx.record │ save │ │ │ read │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ │ │ ▼ │ │ PostRepository (your port, your Tx) │ │ PostSummaryRepository (your port) │ │ │ │ ▲ write │ │ unit of work (#[gateway(unit)]): │ │ PostProjection │ │ begin → handle → append → commit │ │ namespace "summaries" │ │ │ │ │ namespace "notifications" │ │ ▼ │ │ ▲ │ │ EventStore ════════════════════════► TrackingProcessor per namespace │ │ (source of truth, global order) │ │ unit of work: handle + token │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘ └─────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │ handled ▼ ▼ EventFeed (a Stream) QueryUpdateEmitter<Self> catch-up subscriptions subscription queries (live results) Write side. A command goes through a gateway to exactly one handler. The handler finds entities through the application's own repository, lets the domain decide (append events), and records them for the entity they change. The framework's unit of work appends what was recorded, with optimistic concurrency, and commits. The event store is the only source of truth. Every event gets a stream (post-42), a sequence within it, and a global position. Read side. A projection, one per aggregate root, turns committed events into read models and side effects, one namespace each. Queries read the read models, never the store. What connects them is event processing: inline, right after each commit, in the caller's task; or by tracking processors that follow the store on their own tasks, each event in a unit of work that commits the handler's changes with the processor's token.

The blog's PublishPost, on PostgreSQL. The handler is an impl on the gateway, in the use case's file: // src/application/commands/publish_post.rs #[cqrs::command_handler] impl<R: PostRepository, P> CommandHandler<PublishPost> for PostCommandGateway<R, P> { async fn handle( &self, command: &PublishPost, ctx: &mut CommandContext<PostEvent>, tx: &mut R::Tx, ) -> Result<(), BlogError> { let post = self.posts.find(command.id, tx).await?.ok_or(NotFound(command.id))?; post.publish(ctx)?; let post = ctx.record(post); self.posts.save(&post, tx).await?; Ok(()) } } Dispatch. app.commands().send(PublishPost { id }). The gateway (#[cqrs::command_gateway(commands = PostCommands, handles(CreatePost, RetitlePost, PublishPost))]) routes it to its CommandHandler<PublishPost> impl, chosen at compile time. Interceptors added with .intercept(..) wrap the gateway. The unit of work opens. The gateway runs the command in a unit of work of its #[gateway(unit)] field (the unit's Events). Because handle takes tx: &mut R::Tx, the mode is InTransaction<Tx>: the unit begins a transaction and lends it. Without a tx argument the mode is Autocommit: no transaction, one entity per command. The handler decides. It finds the post in its repository (Loaded<Post>: the state and the version it was read at), lets the domain append through ctx (an EventAppender<PostEvent>), and calls ctx.record(post). Recording assigns the appended events to that post and returns it evolved, at its new version; nothing is written yet. The repository saves that state in the same transaction (the SeaORM adapter does; the event-sourced one has Tx = () and saves nothing more). The unit appends and commits. Once handle returns Ok, the unit appends what was recorded, in the transaction, expecting the version the post was loaded at, and commits: the post's row and its events commit together, or not at all. The handler never commits. A lost race reruns the handler. If the stream moved on (or a DCB condition failed), the transaction is rolled back and the handler runs again on fresh state, up to conflict_retries (8 by default). That is why a handler has no side effects besides what it writes in tx: an e-mail belongs in a projection namespace, after the commit. The commit is announced. Events broadcasts the committed envelopes on its live feed, which wakes the tracking processors; an InlinePublisher runs its handlers right away instead. send returns the command's output.

A projection is one struct per aggregate root, holding what its handlers need, with one EventHandler impl per namespace: // src/application/projections/post/mod.rs #[cqrs::projection( name = "post", events = PostEvent, namespaces("summaries", "notifications"), updates(FindPost, ListPublished), subscriptions = PostSubscriptions )] pub struct PostProjection<S, N> { /// Where the summaries are kept. summaries: Arc<S>, /// Who delivers the announcements. notifier: Arc<N>, } Namespaces. Each namespace (#[cqrs::event_handler(namespace = "summaries")]) is run by a tracking processor of its own, named "{projection}.{namespace}" (post.summaries, post.notifications), with its own tokens. A failing notification never holds the read model back. The namespace lives on the projection, not on the event: the domain does not know who consumes it. Tracking processors. A processor reads the log in global order and splits it into segments by stream, so a post's events stay in order and different posts run in parallel (TrackingOptions::segments). Segments are claimed in the TokenStore, so several instances share the work and take over a dead instance's segments. Tokens. A segment's token is a Cursor: the highest position seen, plus the gaps a parallel append left behind. For each event (or batch, with batch = N) the processor opens a unit of work with its TransactionManager, runs the handler and its interceptors, stores the token, and commits. A read model in the same database as the tokens applies each event exactly once; a side effect outside it is at-least-once. Failures. A failing event is rolled back and retried with backoff, holding back only its own segment. With a DeadLetterQueue, after a number of attempts it is parked with the later events of its stream, and everything else keeps flowing. Replay. reset calls each handler's reset (clear the read model) and rewinds the tokens. Namespaces with const REPLAY: bool = false (notifications) skip the replayed events. Inline or asynchronous. The same projection runs either way: Cqrs::from_publisher(InlinePublisher::new(store).with_projection(p)): each namespace sees each commit right after it, in the caller's task, isolated from the others. No runtime, deterministic: what domain and flow tests use. A failing handler does not undo the commit; the failure goes to the publisher's on_failure (LogFailures, logging at error level, by default). Cqrs::new(Events::new(store)).projection(p): commands return once committed, and each namespace follows on its own processor. Read models are eventually consistent; app.settled().await waits for them, and several units together are a tuple ((posts, users).settled().await). On PostgreSQL only the events change: cqrs_postgres::Postgres::new(pool).events::<PostEvent>("posts") gives the same Events with the database's tokens and transactions. Each aggregate root has its own log; all logs share one global position sequence.

A subscription query is the current result of a query, then every update of it. The projection lists its queries in updates(..) and gets one channel per query, QueryUpdateEmitter<Self>. A namespace emits in its updated step: // src/application/projections/post/summaries.rs async fn updated(&self, event: &EventEnvelope<PostEvent>, updates: &QueryUpdateEmitter<Self>) { let Ok(id) = post_of(event) else { return }; if let Ok(Some(summary)) = self.summaries.find(id).await { updates.emit(|query: &FindPost| query.id == id, Some(summary)); } if matches!(event.payload, PostEvent::Published) && let Ok(published) = self.summaries.published().await { updates.emit(|_: &ListPublished| true, published); } } updated runs on every instance, once that namespace handled the event, whichever instance handled it: every subscriber gets the update, wherever it is connected, and never sees a change that was rolled back. Emitting for a query not listed in updates(..) does not compile. A client calls app.queries().subscribe(FindPost { id }): the current result, once the read-model namespaces handled what was committed when the subscription started (so a client sees its own commands), then the updates. subscriptions = PostSubscriptions names the trait the API depends on.

Everything asynchronous about one event type lives behind one value, cqrs::processing::Events<E, S, C, M> (feature tokio): the store S, a live broadcast of committed events, the token store C, the transaction manager M the processors' units of work come from, and the subscription settings. Clones share everything. // In memory: in-memory tokens, units of work `()`. let events = Events::new(InMemoryEventStore::<PostEvent>::new()); // PostgreSQL: the log "posts", tokens and transactions in the database. let events = cqrs_postgres::Postgres::new(pool).events::<PostEvent>("posts"); The same value is three things: the unit of work command gateways run in (see Unit of work): it appends, commits, then broadcasts; the factory of tracking processors: events.projection(p) (one per namespace), events.processor(name, handler), events.track(name, handler); an event feed: events.subscribe(after), the log as a Stream. An application usually never calls the processors' side by hand: Cqrs::new(events)...projection(p).build() starts the projection's processors and keeps their handles (unit.stop(), unit.settled()).

An aggregate root has one projection: a struct holding what its handlers need, with one event handler per namespace. Each namespace runs in a processor of its own, named "{projection}.{namespace}", with its own tokens, its own units of work, its own failures and its own replays: // src/application/projections/post/mod.rs #[cqrs::projection( name = "post", events = PostEvent, namespaces("summaries", "notifications"), updates(FindPost, ListPublished), subscriptions = PostSubscriptions )] pub struct PostProjection<S, N> { /// Where the summaries are kept. summaries: Arc<S>, /// Who delivers the announcements. notifier: Arc<N>, } The blog's two processors are post.summaries (a read model, in batches of 64) and post.notifications (a side effect): // src/application/projections/post/notifications.rs #[cqrs::event_handler(namespace = "notifications")] impl<S: Send + Sync, N: Notifier> EventHandler for PostProjection<S, N> { const REPLAY: bool = false; /// Announces the post if `event` published it. async fn handle( &self, event: &EventEnvelope<PostEvent>, _: &mut ProcessingContext<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerError> { if let PostEvent::Published = event.payload { self.notifier.notify(format!("{} published", event.stream)).await?; } Ok(()) } } Why separate processors: a failing notification holds back only the notifications, never the read model the queries answer from; a replay rebuilds the read model without sending the notifications again (const REPLAY: bool = false); each namespace has the batch that fits it: batch = N on its #[cqrs::event_handler] sets the events per unit of work of its processor (default 1). A namespace whose effects are not undone with its transaction keeps 1, since a failed batch is handled again. This is also where side effects go. A command handler may run again after a lost race, so it must not send the e-mail itself; a namespace with REPLAY = false sends it once the event is committed, at least once. There is no separate kind of "policy": a reaction to events is a namespace. The compiler checks both directions: a namespace listed without its handler, or a handler for a namespace not listed, does not compile. events.projection(p) returns the namespaces' processors to configure: let processors = events.projection(projection) .with_options(TrackingOptions::default().segments(8)); // a namespace's `batch` wins processors.reset().await?; // optional: replay every namespace let running: ProjectionHandle = processors.spawn(); running.namespace("summaries"); // Option<&ProcessorHandle> running.read_models(); // progress of the namespaces that replay running.caught_up(position).await; // every namespace handled `position` running.stop().await; Through the builder, .options(TrackingOptions..) before .projection(..) sets the same.

A TrackingProcessor runs one event handler (or a tuple of them, a processing group) over the whole log, from its stored position: Axon's pooled streaming processor. let processor = events .processor("post-audit", audit) .with_options(TrackingOptions::default().segments(8).batch_size(64)) .with_dead_letters(InMemoryDeadLetters::default(), 5); let handle: ProcessorHandle = processor.spawn(); The handler must fit the processors' unit of work: H: EventHandler<E, M::Tx>, with tokens C: TokenStore<Tx = M::Tx>.

TrackingOptions is built from default(), one setter per field: Setter Default segments 1 Segments the log is split into, by aggregate. Fixed by whoever initializes the token store first. max_segments all At most this many per instance, so several instances share them. claim_timeout 5 s A claim not renewed for this long can be taken over. claim_interval 1 s How often claims are renewed and free segments looked for. retry_initial / retry_max 50 ms / 5 s Backoff between attempts of a failing event, doubling. dead_letter_after None Attempts before parking (set by with_dead_letters). None: retry forever. segment_buffer 1024 Events the shared reader may queue per segment (backpressure). segment_stall_timeout 1 s A segment whose queue stays full this long is detached and reads alone. batch_size 1 Events of a segment handled in one unit of work, with one token update (Axon's batchSize). Takes only what is already waiting; never waits to fill. progress_poll 50 ms How often an instance that does not own every segment reads the others' progress. subscription see below How the store is read. SubscriptionOptions batch_size Events per page read from the store. poll_interval How long to wait for a live event before reading the store anyway. Bounds how late an event whose broadcast was lost, or that another instance committed, is delivered. The live feed carries only this instance's commits. When something relays the others' (on PostgreSQL, Postgres::listen, see guide part 8), it calls Events::committed_elsewhere(), and every subscription and processor of those events reads the store at once instead of waiting for its poll.

Segments. Each event belongs to segment segment_of(stream, segments), a stable hash of the aggregate type and id. Each segment is handled in order by one worker; segments run in parallel. Events of one aggregate are therefore always handled in order, and a failing aggregate holds back only its segment. Shared reader. One reader per instance reads the store once and routes each event to its segment's queue. A full queue is backpressure. A queue that stays full for segment_stall_timeout means the segment is stuck: it is detached and reads on its own, so it never holds the others back. Claims. An instance claims segments in the token store (up to max_segments) and renews them every claim_interval. A crashed instance stops renewing; after claim_timeout another one takes its segments over from their stored positions. PostgreSQL claims use the database's clock, so instances on different machines agree on expiry. Tokens. A segment's token is a Cursor, moved in the same unit of work as the handler's changes. When a segment only sees other segments' events, its token is stored lazily (every 256 events, or after 100 ms idle).

With a batch size above 1, a segment worker takes the events already waiting for it, up to the batch size, and handles them in one unit of work: one transaction, one token update, one commit. Under light load each batch is a single event, so latency does not change; under a backlog (a rebuild, a burst of writes) batches fill up and the cost of the commit is shared. The blog's summaries rebuild 5000 events in 0.25 s with batch = 64, against 4.6 s one by one. A failed batch is rolled back and its events are handled one at a time, each with the usual retries and dead letters; a batch with an event of a parked aggregate goes one at a time from the start. Batch only a handler whose effects are all undone with its transaction.

Without dead letters, a failing event is retried forever with backoff, holding back its segment (status().failing says why). With with_dead_letters(queue, after), an event that failed after times is parked, keyed by its aggregate (the "sequence"); every later event of that aggregate is parked behind it without being tried, so the aggregate's order is kept, and the segment moves on. let outcome = processor.retry_dead_letters().await?; // once the cause is fixed // outcome.handled, outcome.still_parked, outcome.evicted A projection takes a queue for all its namespaces, each parking under its own processor's name: events.projection(p).with_dead_letters(queue, after), or .projection_with(p, |processors| processors.with_dead_letters(queue, after)) on the Cqrs builder. Its retry_dead_letters() retries every namespace and returns each one's outcome. Each sequence is retried oldest first, each event in its own unit of work, and stops at its first failure. retry_dead_letters(queue, name, &transactions, &handler, &policy) does the same without a processor. The enqueue policy​ with_dead_letters(queue, after) parks after after failures and keeps a parked letter until a retry handles it: the policy ParkAfter(after). Any other rule is an EnqueuePolicy (Axon 5's), asked after each failed attempt of an event and at each failed retry of a parked one: let policy = |letter: &DeadLetter<PostEvent>, cause: &HandlerError| match letter.is_parked() { // A refusal will not get better: skip the event, do not park it. false if cause.to_string().contains("422") => EnqueueDecision::Ignore, false if letter.attempts >= 3 => EnqueueDecision::Enqueue(Metadata::from([("target", "mailer")])), false => EnqueueDecision::Retry, // Parked: give up after ten failed retries. true if letter.attempts >= 10 => EnqueueDecision::Evict, true => EnqueueDecision::Requeue(letter.diagnostics.clone()), }; let processor = events.processor("mailer", mailer).with_dead_letters(queue, 3).with_enqueue_policy(policy); Decision A failing event A parked one, failing again at a retry Retry tried again after a backoff kept Enqueue(diagnostics) parked, its aggregate's later events behind it kept Requeue(diagnostics) parked kept, with these diagnostics and last_touched Evict / Ignore skipped: the segment moves past it, unhandled removed: the sequence's next letter comes first A letter carries what the policy needs and keeps: attempts, parked_at, last_touched and diagnostics (stored in cqrs_dead_letters on PostgreSQL). A projection takes one policy for all its namespaces: processors.with_dead_letters(queue, 3).with_enqueue_policy(policy). A queue goes with the units of work it can join: Queue Goes with InMemoryDeadLetters Tx = () (in-memory tokens) lost when the process ends, with the tokens cqrs_postgres::PostgresDeadLetters::new(store) PgTransaction table cqrs_dead_letters; the event is read back from store's log your own DeadLetterQueue<E, Tx> The compiler refuses an in-memory queue with a database's tokens: the token would move past a parked event that a restart then forgets. A letter enters the queue in the unit of work that moves the token past its event, and leaves it in the one that applies it, so a crash can neither lose a letter nor apply its event twice. If the queue cannot say whether an aggregate is parked, the processor waits and asks again rather than handle an event ahead of the parked ones. A queue is given to a processor made with events.processor(..), or to a projection's namespaces (events.projection(..).with_dead_letters(..), Cqrs::projection_with). Without one, failing events are retried until they succeed.

// every instance stopped events.projection(PostProjection::new(..)).reset().await?; // tokens to 0, then each handler's reset // then spawn (or build the unit) again: it replays reset moves every segment's token back to the start, marks the events stored so far as a replay, then runs the handler's reset in a unit of work of its own (a read model clears its tables there). It fails with ResetError::Running while any instance holds a segment. During the replay context.replay() is true, and namespaces with const REPLAY: bool = false skip those events, so the notifications are not sent again.

processor.run(shutdown) is a future: it claims segments, handles their events, and, once shutdown completes, finishes the events in hand and releases its segments for other instances. The caller runs it (awaited, or in a JoinSet with the rest of the application); the segments' workers run on Tokio tasks of the current runtime. let progress = processor.progress(); tasks.spawn(processor.run(shutdown.cancelled_owned())); processor.spawn() does that on a Tokio task and returns a ProcessorHandle: handle.status(); // ProcessorStatus handle.caught_up(position).await; // this instance's segments handled `position` handle.stop().await; // after the events in hand; releases the claims handle.abort().await; // as a crash would: claims expire, others take over

ProcessorStatus is what an instance reports: position (the lowest watermark of its segments), failing (the error of an event being retried), segments, cursors, segment_count, and shared_cursors (the stored cursor of every segment, read every progress_poll while this instance does not own them all). status.covers(p): this instance's segments saw position p. status.handled(p): the processor handled p in any of its instances (from its own segments when it owns them all, from the shared cursors otherwise). What a reader waits for. ProcessorProgress::of(&handle) waits on handled; GlobalProgress (events.global_progress(name)) reads the token store alone, for a process that does not run the processor. unit.settled().await waits until every processor of a Cqrs unit handled everything committed before the call ((posts, users).settled() for several roots).

events.subscribe(after) (the EventFeed port, or cqrs::store::subscribe) is a Stream of every committed event with position > after, each once, in position order, then the new ones as they commit. It reads the store in pages and follows the live broadcast, going back to the store whenever the broadcast lags or misses something, and reads through a gap-aware Cursor, so appends committing out of order are never skipped. It keeps no token: the consumer remembers its last position.

Subscription queries come from the projection: updates(FindPost, ListPublished) gives it one channel per query, and a namespace emits in updated(&self, event, updates: &QueryUpdateEmitter<Self>) once it handled the event. The Cqrs unit runs an emitter per such namespace on every instance, so a subscriber connected to any instance sees every change, and app.queries().subscribe(FindPost { id }) yields the current result, once the read models caught up with what was committed, then the updates. See part 6 of the guide.

Without a runtime, an InlinePublisher runs the handlers in the caller's task, right after each commit: // src/config.rs let projection = PostProjection::new(Arc::clone(&summaries), Arc::clone(&notifier)); let publisher = InlinePublisher::<PostEvent, _, _>::new(store.clone()).with_projection(projection); let blog = Cqrs::from_publisher(publisher) .commands(|events| PostCommandGateway::new(posts_over(&store), events)) .queries(PostQueryGateway::new(Arc::clone(&summaries))) .build(); A command returns once every handler ran (handle, then committed), so queries see its effects at once. What is fed: with_projection(p) each namespace sees the whole commit, isolated from the others; no replays inline with_processor((a, b)) a group: members in order, a failure stopping the group with_processor(Isolated((a, b))) each handler on its own: one failing neither stops nor delays the other A failing handler skips the rest of that commit, so it never sees events out of order. Failures never undo the commit, and there is nobody to return them to (the events are stored): they go to the publisher's OnFailure policy, LogFailures by default (logs at error level), or any Fn(&ProcessingFailure) given to on_failure(..). No tokens, no retries: for tests and simple applications.

CQRS and event sourcing for Rust, modeled on Axon Framework 5. It is a library, not a framework. The application owns its repositories, its database and its transactions, and lends them to the handlers. The library runs the parts that are easy to get wrong: the unit of work around a command (append what was decided, commit, retry a lost race), and the processors that turn committed events into read models, each with its token, its transaction and its dead letters. Everything is dispatched statically. There is no handler registry behind dyn, no Box<dyn Future>, no Any and no TypeId: routing a command to its handler, wiring a projection's namespaces to their processors, chaining interceptors, all of it is resolved by the type checker. The running code is plain function calls, and the mistakes a registry finds at startup are compile errors here: a command listed in a gateway's handles(..) without its CommandHandler impl; a projection namespace without its event handler (the projection cannot be wired), or a handler for a namespace the projection does not list; an update emitted for a query the projection does not list in updates(..); an entity recorded with events of another aggregate's type. It is async from the ground up: every contract is a Future or a Stream, and committed events are a Stream you can hand to axum, async-graphql or a Tokio task.

An account opened and credited through commands; its balance, a read model kept by a projection, answered by a query. In memory and without a runtime: the projection runs inline, right after each commit. This is the quickstart of the crate's rustdoc, which compiles and runs as a test. The domain: what happened to an account, and the account deciding. use std::{collections::HashMap, sync::{Arc, Mutex}}; use cqrs::{ Cqrs, aggregate::AggregateLoader, prelude::*, processing::InlinePublisher, store::{InMemoryEventStore, StoreError}, testing::block_on, }; #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, cqrs::DomainEvent)] enum AccountEvent { Opened, Deposited { amount: u64 }, } #[cqrs::aggregate(name = "account", event = AccountEvent)] struct Account { id: u32, balance: u64 } impl Account { fn apply(&mut self, event: &AccountEvent) { if let AccountEvent::Deposited { amount } = event { self.balance += amount; } } fn deposit(&self, amount: u64, events: &mut impl EventAppender) -> Result<(), BankError> { if amount == 0 { return Err(BankError::NothingToDeposit); } events.append(AccountEvent::Deposited { amount }); Ok(()) } } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq)] enum BankError { NothingToDeposit, NoSuchAccount, Store(String) } impl From for BankError { fn from(error: StoreError) -> Self { Self::Store(error.to_string()) } } The commands, and the gateway handling them, one impl each. The gateway is the handler: one struct with what its commands need, and the unit of work they run in (#[gateway(unit)]). A handler appends through its CommandContext and records the entity the events belong to; it never commits. #[cqrs::command(error = BankError)] struct Open { id: u32 } #[cqrs::command(error = BankError)] struct Deposit { id: u32, amount: u64 } #[cqrs::command_gateway(handles(Open, Deposit))] struct Bank

{ accounts: AggregateLoader>, #[gateway(unit)] events: P, } #[cqrs::command_handler] impl

CommandHandler for Bank

{ async fn handle(&self, command: &Open, ctx: &mut CommandContext) -> Result<(), BankError> { ctx.append(AccountEvent::Opened); ctx.record(New::(command.id)); // a new stream: fails if it exists Ok(()) } } #[cqrs::command_handler] impl

CommandHandler for Bank

{ async fn handle(&self, command: &Deposit, ctx: &mut CommandContext) -> Result<(), BankError> { let account = self.accounts.load(&command.id).await?.ok_or(BankError::NoSuchAccount)?; account.deposit(command.amount, ctx)?; ctx.record(account); // appended and committed once the handler returns Ok(()) } } The read side: a projection keeps the balances, a query reads them. type Balances = Arc>>; #[cqrs::projection(name = "account", events = AccountEvent, namespaces("balances"))] struct AccountProjection { balances: Balances } #[cqrs::event_handler(namespace = "balances")] impl EventHandler for AccountProjection { async fn handle(&self, event: &EventEnvelope, _: &mut ProcessingContext<'_>) -> Result<(), HandlerError> { let id = event.aggregate_id::().ok_or_else(|| HandlerError::msg("not an account"))?; let mut balances = self.balances.lock().unwrap(); let balance = balances.entry(id).or_default(); if let AccountEvent::Deposited { amount } = event.payload { *balance += amount; } Ok(()) } } #[cqrs::query(output = Option, error = BankError)] struct Balance { id: u32 } #[cqrs::query_gateway(handles(Balance))] struct Accounts { balances: Balances } #[cqrs::query_handler] impl QueryHandler for Accounts { async fn handle(&self, query: Balance) -> Result, BankError> { Ok(self.balances.lock().unwrap().get(&query.id).copied()) } } Wiring: the store, the publisher running the projection inline, and the application's unit (Cqrs), built by a typed builder. fn main() -> Result<(), BankError> { let store = InMemoryEventStore::new(); let balances = Balances::default(); let publisher = InlinePublisher::new(store.clone()) .with_projection(AccountProjection { balances: Arc::clone(&balances) }); let bank = Cqrs::from_publisher(publisher) .commands(|events| Bank { accounts: AggregateLoader::new(store), events }) .queries(Accounts { balances }) .build(); block_on(async { bank.commands().send(Open { id: 1 }).await?; bank.commands().send(Deposit { id: 1, amount: 30 }).await?; assert_eq!(bank.commands().send(Deposit { id: 1, amount: 0 }).await, Err(BankError::NothingToDeposit)); assert_eq!(bank.queries().query(Balance { id: 1 }).await?, Some(30)); Ok::<(), BankError>(()) }) } Going asynchronous changes only the wiring: Cqrs::new(Events::new(store)) instead of Cqrs::from_publisher(..), and .projection(..) on the builder, which runs each namespace in a tracking processor of its own. The guide takes that step, and the next ones.

These hold everywhere in the library, and are worth keeping in an application built on it: Static dispatch. Heterogeneous collections are tuples; extension points are generic parameters. See Patterns § Static dispatch. Macros only write what you could write by hand: trait impls, associated types, and the traits and types their callers name (the gateway's commands = PostCommands, the projection's update channels). None adds fields to your types, and each documents its hand-written equivalent. The domain does not know the framework. An aggregate is a struct; its decisions take &mut impl EventAppender<E>, and its state changes only in apply (Aggregate::evolve). The framework commits, not the handler. A command handler records what it decided; the unit of work appends and commits, and runs the handler again after a lost race. So a handler has no side effects: those belong in a projection namespace, after the commit. The store is the source of truth. Read models, live feeds, query updates and snapshots can be lost and rebuilt from it.

Architecture: the modules, how a command becomes a read-model row, and how each Axon 5 concept maps to this library. Guide: build a blog step by step, from the domain to a GraphQL API on PostgreSQL. The finished code is examples/blog. Patterns: the small design patterns the library is made of, one section each. examples/bank puts two of them to work in a second application: a bank behind a REST API (axum) whose portfolios are projected from two logs (fan-in), and whose accounts' log reaches a compliance service through RabbitMQ (the log as an outbox). Reference: Unit of work: what commits when, on both sides. Event processing: tracking processors, segments, tokens, replay, dead letters, subscriptions. Storage: the store ports, in memory and PostgreSQL, cursors, snapshots and upcasting. Performance: benchmarks and the cost of each abstraction.

The library is made of small, repeatable patterns. Each section below names one, says what problem it solves, shows its shape, and lists its rules. Applications use the same patterns, so the sections double as a style guide. Snippets marked // src/... or // tests/... come from examples/blog. Static dispatch: 1–6 Messages and gateways: 7–10 Domain: 11–16 Command handling: 17–20 Storage: 21–23 Event handling: 24–30 Interceptors: 31–32 Read side and streams: 33–35 Testing: 36–38 Composition: 39

Problem. Async traits usually box their futures (Pin<Box<dyn Future>>): an allocation and a virtual call per call, and Send hidden. Shape. Every async contract returns impl Future<Output = ...> + Send; implementations write a plain async fn. // src/application/commands/post_repository.rs fn find(&self, id: PostId, tx: &mut Self::Tx) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Option<Loaded<Post>>, StoreError>> + Send; // src/infrastructure/event_sourced_post_repository.rs async fn find(&self, id: PostId, (): &mut ()) -> Result<Option<Loaded<Post>>, StoreError> { self.loader.load(&id).await } Rules. The + Send makes tokio::spawn-ability part of the contract: an implementation holding a non-Send value across an .await does not compile. Such traits are not object-safe, which is the point: nothing here is a trait object.

Problem. "A list of handlers of different types" is Vec<Box<dyn Handler>> in most frameworks. Shape. The trait is implemented for tuples (up to 8 members); each member keeps its type, and the tuple calls them in order. events.processor("read-models", (Search::new(..), Stats::new(..))).spawn(); // a processing group Intercepted::new(gateway, (Tracing, Timing, RequireUser)); // first outermost store.with_upcasters((upcast("post.created", 1, ..), upcast("post.created", 2, ..))); (posts, users).settled().await; // one unit per root Rules. A tuple of event handlers is a group everywhere: one token, one unit of work, all or none, the first failure stopping the rest; in a replay, members with REPLAY = false are skipped. Inline, where each handler should see every event whatever the others do, wrap it: Isolated((a, b)).

Problem. Sharing a component (Arc<T>, &T) must not change its behavior, but a blanket impl that forwards only the required methods silently drops the overrides of provided ones. Shape. Every forwarding impl forwards every method, checked by the compiler: // Forwards every method, so an override of a provided one is never lost. #[deny(clippy::missing_trait_methods)] impl<E: DomainEvent, U: UnitMode, T: UnitOfWork<E, U>> UnitOfWork<E, U> for std::sync::Arc<T> { .. } Rules. Applies to every trait with provided methods (EventHandler, UnitOfWork, EventPublisher, Dispatch...).

Problem. Pluggable parts (store, tokens, transactions, snapshots) are usually injected as trait objects. Shape. Type parameters with defaults, swapped by builder methods that change the type: pub struct AggregateLoader<A, S, N = ()> { .. } // store, snapshots pub struct Events<E, S, C = InMemoryTokenStore, M = ()> { .. } // store, tokens, transactions AggregateLoader::<Post, _>::new(store).with_snapshots(InMemorySnapshots::default(), 50); Events::new(store).with_tokens(tokens).with_transactions(transactions); Rules. () is the "nothing" of most ports (no snapshots, no transaction, no upcaster). The composition root never names the resulting types: the builder infers them.

Problem. Static routing turns mistakes into trait errors, cryptic by default. Shape. #[diagnostic::on_unimplemented] on the routing traits, and spanned errors from the macros: error[E0277]: `Clock

` lists `Ring` in `handles(...)` but has no handler for it | 15 | struct Clock

{ | ^^^^^^^^ no `#[cqrs::command_handler]` / `#[cqrs::query_handler]` impl for `Ring` Rules. Add one wherever a user meets a trait bound instead of a function. The macros' messages are checked by UI tests (crates/cqrs/tests/ui).

documents.t: Problem. Macros that inject fields or rewrite types make code unreadable without expanding them, and lock users in. Shape. Every macro emits trait impls and associated types; each one's rustdoc shows the hand-written equivalent: Macro Writes #[cqrs::aggregate] impl Aggregate #[cqrs::command], #[cqrs::query] impl Message and the Command / Query marker #[derive(cqrs::DomainEvent)] event_type, event_version, TagResolver from #[tag] fields #[cqrs::command_gateway], #[cqrs::query_gateway] impl Dispatch<M> per message listed, the check that each has a handler, the generated trait #[cqrs::command_handler], #[cqrs::query_handler] the Handles<M> marker; for commands, type Event and type Unit read from handle #[cqrs::projection] impl Projection, impl Route<Tx> (namespace to handler), the updates' channels #[cqrs::event_handler] the event and unit-of-work generics; with namespace, that namespace's handler Rules. Nothing a macro does is required: a domain that wants no attributes implements Aggregate and DomainEvent itself.
documents.s: 6. Macros only write what a user could

documents.t: Problem. If handlers declare what they return, a caller must know which handler answers a message to know what comes back. Shape. // src/application/commands/create_post.rs #[cqrs::command(output = PostId, error = BlogError)] // output defaults to () pub struct CreatePost { pub title: String } // src/application/queries/find_post.rs #[cqrs::query(output = Option<PostSummary>, error = BlogError)] pub struct FindPost { pub id: PostId } gateway.send(CreatePost { .. }) returns Result<PostId, BlogError>, whoever handles it. Rules. Sending a query with .send (or a command with .query) is a compile error: the Command and Query markers keep the sides apart.
documents.s: 7. The message owns its output and error

documents.t: Problem. Registries keyed by TypeId fail at runtime when a handler is missing or registered twice; one class per handler multiplies the dependencies to pass around. Shape. One struct per side holds what its use cases need and lists the messages it routes; each message has its own impl, in the use case's file: // src/application/commands/mod.rs #[cqrs::command_gateway(commands = PostCommands, handles(CreatePost, RetitlePost, PublishPost))] pub struct PostCommandGateway<R, P> { posts: R, #[gateway(unit)] events: P, } // src/application/commands/publish_post.rs #[cqrs::command_handler] impl<R: PostRepository, P> CommandHandler<PublishPost> for PostCommandGateway<R, P> { async fn handle( &self, command: &PublishPost, ctx: &mut CommandContext<PostEvent>, tx: &mut R::Tx, ) -> Result<(), BlogError> { let post = self.posts.find(command.id, tx).await?.ok_or(NotFound(command.id))?; post.publish(ctx)?; let post = ctx.record(post); self.posts.save(&post, tx).await?; Ok(()) } } Queries are the same: #[cqrs::query_gateway(queries = PostQueries, handles(FindPost, ListPublished))] on PostQueryGateway<M>, one #[cqrs::query_handler] impl QueryHandler<FindPost> per query. Rules. A message listed without its impl, or listed twice, does not compile where the gateway is declared; one not listed is E0277 where it is sent. A command gateway needs a #[gateway(unit)] field: the unit of work its commands run in. Commands are taken by reference: a handler may run again.

Problem. Code that sends every command of a module (an API, a test double, a return type) would repeat one CommandGateway<_> bound per command wherever it is needed. Shape. commands = PostCommands generates a trait bounded by CommandGateway of each command listed, implemented by everything that routes them; queries = PostQueries the same with QueryGateway, and the projection's subscriptions = PostSubscriptions with QuerySubscriptions. Code that needs fewer names only those: // src/presentation/mod.rs pub trait BlogApi: Send + Sync + 'static { type Commands: PostCommands; type Queries: PostQueries + PostSubscriptions; type Events: EventFeed<PostEvent>; // .. } // tests/flow.rs pub async fn create_and_publish<G>(gateway: &G, title: &str) -> Result<PostId, BlogError> where G: CommandGateway<CreatePost> + CommandGateway<PublishPost>, { .. } Rules. Whatever stands behind the gateway (interceptors, a unit) still implements them, so code written against them compiles against the in-memory app, the PostgreSQL app and test doubles alike.

Problem. Who asked, and why, should travel with the events a command causes, without every handler passing it along. Shape. Send with metadata; every event recorded in that run stores it. // src/presentation/http.rs let mut metadata = Metadata::new(); metadata.insert("correlation_id".to_owned(), id.to_owned()); // in a resolver app.commands().send_with(PublishPost { id }, metadata).await?; Rules. Interceptors see and may change it before the handler (pattern 33); handlers read it with ctx.metadata(); event handlers find it in event.metadata.

Problem. Aggregates that mutate themselves in command methods can change state without recording an event, and carry a pending-events buffer that leaks into serialization. Shape. State changes only in evolve (here, apply); decisions borrow immutably and append. A creation has no instance to decide on, so it is an associated function: // src/domain/post/mod.rs impl Post { fn apply(&mut self, event: &PostEvent) { // the only mutation match event { PostEvent::Created { title, .. } | PostEvent::Retitled { title } => self.title.clone_from(title), PostEvent::Published => self.published = true, } } pub fn create(id: PostId, title: impl Into<String>, events: &mut impl EventAppender<PostEvent>) -> Result<(), PostError> { let title = valid_title(title.into())?; events.append(PostEvent::Created { id, title }); Ok(()) } pub fn publish(&self, events: &mut impl EventAppender<PostEvent>) -> Result<(), PostError> { if self.published { return Err(PostError::AlreadyPublished); } events.append(PostEvent::Published); Ok(()) } } Rules. evolve never validates, fails or does I/O: it runs on replay too. A decision sees the state from before it ran; assigning a field in one is a compile error (E0594). EventAppender<E> is implemented for every Extend<E> + Send, so a test passes a Vec, and a domain can take impl Extend<PostEvent> and not depend on the library.

// src/domain/post/mod.rs #[cqrs::aggregate(name = "post", event = PostEvent)] #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)] pub struct Post { id: PostId, title: String, published: bool } Writes impl Aggregate: TYPE from name, Id from the id field (or the one marked #[aggregate(id)]), initial with the other fields at Default, evolve calling apply. Rules. TYPE prefixes stream ids (post-42): changing it orphans stored streams. Id: Display renders the suffix and must be stable; a projection parses it back with event.aggregate_id::<Post>().

Problem. The version used for optimistic concurrency is persistence data; in the domain struct it mixes concerns, and reusing a stale aggregate is a classic bug. Shape. Loaded<A> wraps the state with the version it was read at and derefs to &A only (no &mut: E0596). ctx.record(entity) takes it by value and returns it evolved, at its new version. A creation records New<A>, which expects the stream not to exist: // src/application/commands/create_post.rs let id = self.posts.next_id(tx).await?; Post::create(id, command.title.as_str(), ctx)?; let post = ctx.record(New::<Post>(id)); // Loaded<Post>, after `Created` self.posts.save(&post, tx).await?; Rules. The version travels from find to the append without the domain seeing it. A repository that stores state builds one with Loaded::at(post, version). To create what is missing (a counter starting at zero), decide on find(..).await?.unwrap_or_else(|| New(id).into()).
documents.s: 13. The loaded aggregate carries its version

documents.t: // src/domain/post/event.rs #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize, cqrs::DomainEvent)] pub enum PostEvent { #[event(name = "post.created")] Created { id: PostId, title: String }, #[event(name = "post.retitled")] Retitled { title: String }, #[event(name = "post.published")] Published, } // crates/cqrs/tests/dcb.rs #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, cqrs::DomainEvent)] enum SchoolEvent { #[event(name = "student.subscribed")] Subscribed { #[tag] course: u32, #[tag] student: u32 }, // .. } Rules. The stored type is the name, so renaming a variant is free. Each variant is versioned on its own (#[event(version = 2)], default 1): bump it when the payload's shape changes and add an upcaster. #[tag] fields become the event's tags (keyed by field name, or #[tag = "key"]); without any, it has none. To resolve tags by hand, implement DomainEvent and TagResolver yourself.
documents.s: 14. Stable event names, versions and tags

documents.t: Problem. A rule spanning two aggregates (a course's capacity and a student's course limit) forces a bigger aggregate or a saga. Shape. Each aggregate is built from the events tagged with its id, whatever stream holds them; the handler loads both with load_in, and the append is conditional on neither having changed: // crates/cqrs/tests/dcb.rs #[cqrs::aggregate(event = SchoolEvent, tag = "course")] struct Course { id: u32, capacity: usize, students: Vec<u32> } #[cqrs::aggregate(event = SchoolEvent, tag = "student")] struct Student { #[aggregate(id)] id: u32, courses: usize } // in the handler, for each course; `courses` and `students` are AggregateLoaders let course = self.courses.load_in(&course, events).await?.ok_or(Error::NoSuchCourse)?; let student = self.students.load_in(&command.student, events).await?; // read only: still checked course.subscribe(command.student, student.as_deref(), events)?; events.record(course); // ConditionFailed at the append if either changed Without an aggregate, ctx.source(&store, EventCriteria::tagged([..])) reads by criteria and conditions the run's appends the same way. Rules. load_in adds a condition even when the aggregate does not exist yet: absence is a fact too. A failed condition is a lost race: the handler runs again. On PostgreSQL, decisions on different tags run in parallel, on the same tag they take turns (pattern 23).
documents.s: 15. Aggregates built from tags (dynamic consistency boundaries)

documents.t: // src/application/error.rs pub enum BlogError { Domain(PostError), NotFound(PostId), Conflict, Store(String) } impl From<PostError> for BlogError { .. } impl From<NotFound<PostId>> for BlogError { .. } impl From<StoreError> for BlogError { /* Conflict | ConditionFailed => Conflict, other => Store */ } Rules. The domain returns its own enum; the application error classifies by origin, so ? maps it and an adapter picks a status code without parsing strings. A domain error means nothing was appended. A command's error converts From<StoreError>: the unit of work's failures reach the caller through it.
documents.s: 16. Domain errors are values, not store errors

documents.t: Problem. A handler that commits can commit twice, commit half, or forget; a repository that stores state must write in the events' transaction. Shape. The gateway hands each run a fresh CommandContext<E>: ctx.append(e) an event, until record assigns it ctx.record(entity) the events so far are entity's; returns it evolved (nothing written yet) ctx.metadata() the command's metadata ctx.source(&store, criteria), ctx.depend_on(condition) conditions the appends on what was read Once handle returns Ok, the unit of work appends what was recorded and commits. The signature picks its mode: no tx argument: Autocommit, one append statement, one entity; tx: &mut Tx: InTransaction<Tx>. The unit opens the transaction, the handler and its repositories write in it, the events are appended last, and everything commits together, or nothing does. Rules. The handler never commits nor announces: once committed, the unit hands the events to the processors. Events appended but not recorded are a forgotten record (debug builds panic). Recording two entities in Autocommit is an error: take the tx. See Unit of work § The command side.
documents.s: 17. The handler records, the framework commits

documents.t: Shape. When the append fails with a version conflict, or ConditionFailed, the unit rolls back and runs the handler again on fresh state, up to conflict_retries() times (default 8): #[cqrs::command_handler] impl<R: PostRepository, P> CommandHandler<RetitlePost> for PostCommandGateway<R, P> { async fn handle(..) -> Result<(), BlogError> { .. } fn conflict_retries(&self) -> u32 { 0 } // let the caller retry instead } Rules. New on an existing stream is not a race: it fails at once. In a unit that cannot roll back (in memory), a run that appended part of its writes is not re-run: the conflict reaches the caller. Because a handler may run more than once, it has no side effects besides what it writes in tx: an e-mail or a broker message goes to a namespace that does not replay.
documents.s: 18. Re-run on a lost race, without side effects

documents.t: Problem. A framework-defined Repository<A> dictates what every repository looks like; real ones have the finders their use cases need, and store state their own way. Shape. The application declares the port, working in the unit's transaction; infrastructure adapts it: // src/application/commands/post_repository.rs pub trait PostRepository: Send + Sync { type Tx: Send; fn next_id(&self, tx: &mut Self::Tx) -> impl Future<Output = Result<PostId, StoreError>> + Send; fn find(&self, id: PostId, tx: &mut Self::Tx) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Option<Loaded<Post>>, StoreError>> + Send; fn save(&self, post: &Loaded<Post>, tx: &mut Self::Tx) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), StoreError>> + Send; } EventSourcedPostRepository (Tx = ()) rebuilds posts with an AggregateLoader; its save writes nothing. SeaOrmPostRepository (Tx = PgTransaction) keeps each post in a table, with SeaORM, in the transaction the events are appended in; the row keeps the stream version, so concurrent changes still conflict. Rules. Handlers take only their services (R: PostRepository); the library never builds the repository. Events are appended by the unit only.
documents.s: 19. Your repository, in the unit's transaction

documents.t: Problem. "Remind the author in three days", "close the auction at noon": a decision now, a command later. Kept in memory, a schedule is lost at the next deploy; sent from a timer in the handler, it is a side effect a re-run repeats. Shape. A CommandSchedule<C, Tx> per command type keeps them; the handler schedules within its unit of work, and deliver_scheduled sends what is due through the gateway: #[cqrs::command_handler] impl<R: PostRepository, S: CommandSchedule<RemindAuthor, R::Tx>, P> CommandHandler<CreatePost> for PostCommandGateway<R, S, P> { async fn handle(&self, command: &CreatePost, ctx: &mut CommandContext<PostEvent>, tx: &mut R::Tx) -> Result<PostId, BlogError> { // ... decide and record ... let due = SystemTime::now() + Duration::from_secs(3 * 24 * 3600); self.reminders.schedule_in(tx, due, &RemindAuthor { id }, ctx.metadata()).await?; Ok(id) } } // On every instance: claims what is due, sends it through `gateway` (any // CommandGateway<RemindAuthor>), removes what was handled. deliver_scheduled(pg.schedule::<RemindAuthor>("reminders"), gateway, DeliveryOptions::default(), shutdown).await; Rules. The schedule commits with the events, or not at all (a re-run after a lost race schedules once). Delivery is at least once and the command's handler decides again on the state it finds then; a failure is tried again with backoff and given up after max_attempts, kept with its error. On PostgreSQL (PostgresSchedule, table cqrs_scheduled) times are the database's and deliverers on several instances claim different commands (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED). cancel and reschedule take the ScheduleToken that scheduling returned. (Axon 5 removed its schedulers; this is the shape of Axon 4's CommandScheduler.)

// src/config.rs EventSourcedPostRepository::new(store.clone()).with_snapshots(InMemorySnapshots::default(), SNAPSHOT_EVERY) // inside: AggregateLoader::with_snapshots; on PostgreSQL, PostgresSnapshotStore::new(pool) A load starts from the newest snapshot and replays the rest; one that replayed every events or more saves a new one. Appends never do. Rules. An optimization, never the truth: deleting snapshots only costs time, and one that fails to load or save is a warning and a full replay. Bump PostgresSnapshotStore::with_revision when the aggregate's shape changes, so old snapshots are ignored. A repository that stores state in a table needs none.

Problem. Every store would re-implement the same steps around its write: skip empty batches, resolve tags, build envelopes. Shape. AppendEvents::append_if is provided: nothing to append succeeds at once, tags are resolved, the envelopes are built. A store writes only append_tagged: the tagged events, atomically with the version check and the condition, returning what it recorded (position, sequence, time). Rules. What must be identical across stores lives in the provided method, tested once. One port per capability (LoadStream, AppendEvents, SourceEvents, ReadLog); EventStore is all four. See Storage § Writing a store.

Gap-aware cursor. Parallel appends can commit a later position before an earlier one, so a reader keeps Cursor { position, gaps }, and gives a gap up only once every transaction that could fill it has ended (Storage § Global order). Locks derived from the domain. An append takes shared advisory locks on its events' tags and types; a criterion read for a conditional append takes its keys exclusively. Only decisions on the same tags wait for each other (Storage § Locks). Checked SQL. Every statement is sqlx::query!, checked at build time through CQRS_POSTGRES_URL (never an application's DATABASE_URL) or the committed .sqlx/ cache.

let store = PostgresEventStore::<PostEvent>::new(pool, "posts").with_upcasters(( upcast("post.created", 1, |payload| payload["Created"]["tags"] = json!([])), upcast("post.created", 2, |payload| payload["Created"]["draft"] = json!(true)), )); Each upcast(type, from_version, fn) rewrites the JSON of one version into the next; a tuple chains them. Stored rows never change, and an event no upcaster applies to is decoded directly. Rules. Upcasters belong to the store, so a log with old shapes is wired with Events::new(pg.store(log).with_upcasters(..)) and the Postgres tokens and transactions, instead of pg.events(log). See Storage § Upcasting.

Problem. Read models, notifications and integrations all "react to committed events", but frameworks often give them different interfaces. Shape. One trait, Axon 5's event handling component: pub trait EventHandler<E: DomainEvent, Tx: Send = ()>: Send + Sync { const REPLAY: bool = true; fn handle(&self, event: &EventEnvelope<E>, context: &mut ProcessingContext<'_, Tx>) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerError>> + Send; fn committed(&self, event: &EventEnvelope<E>) -> impl Future<Output = ()> + Send { async {} } fn reset(&self, context: &mut ProcessingContext<'_, Tx>) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerError>> + Send { async { Ok(()) } } } committed runs after the unit of work committed, only if it did; reset clears what was built before a replay. Rules. handle may run more than once for an event (retries, a failed batch): make it transactional or idempotent (event.position is a deduplication key). HandlerError converts from any std::error::Error, so ? works.

Problem. A projection writing SQL must run in the processor's transaction; one that writes to memory should run with any token store. Shape. ProcessingContext<'_, Tx> carries the unit of work (context.transaction()) and whether the event is a replay (context.replay()). Name Tx to require it; leave it generic to accept any: // src/application/projections/post/summaries.rs #[cqrs::event_handler(namespace = "summaries", batch = 64)] impl<S, N, Tx> EventHandler for PostProjection<S, N> where S: PostSummaryRepository + PostSummaryStore<Tx>, N: Send + Sync, Tx: Send, { async fn handle(&self, event: &EventEnvelope<PostEvent>, context: &mut ProcessingContext<'_, Tx>) -> Result<(), HandlerError> { let tx = context.transaction(); // () in memory, PgTransaction on PostgreSQL // self.summaries.save(tx, ..) / update(tx, ..) } } Rules. A handler whose context names no Tx is made generic by the macro. One that names PgTransaction over in-memory tokens is a compile error ("cannot run in units of work"). What it writes in the transaction commits with the processor's token: applied exactly once.
documents.s: 26. The handler names its unit of work

documents.t: Problem. One processor per read model multiplies the wiring; one for everything couples a slow side effect to the read models. Shape. The projection is a struct holding what its handlers need. It lists its namespaces; each has its own handler impl and its own processor ("post.summaries", "post.notifications"), with its own tokens: // src/application/projections/post/mod.rs #[cqrs::projection( name = "post", events = PostEvent, namespaces("summaries", "notifications"), updates(FindPost, ListPublished), subscriptions = PostSubscriptions )] pub struct PostProjection<S, N> { summaries: Arc<S>, notifier: Arc<N>, } Rules. Checked both ways at compile time: a namespace listed without a handler does not run, a handler for an unlisted namespace does not compile. Renaming the projection or a namespace starts its processor over (new tokens). The namespace belongs to the projection, not the event: the domain does not know who consumes it.
documents.s: 27. One projection per aggregate root, a processor per namespace

documents.t: Problem. A notification sent from a command handler is sent again when the handler re-runs, or even if the commit fails; one sent from a read model's handler is sent again on every rebuild. Shape. A namespace of the projection with REPLAY = false: // src/application/projections/post/notifications.rs #[cqrs::event_handler(namespace = "notifications")] impl<S: Send + Sync, N: Notifier> EventHandler for PostProjection<S, N> { const REPLAY: bool = false; async fn handle(&self, event: &EventEnvelope<PostEvent>, _: &mut ProcessingContext<'_>) -> Result<(), HandlerError> { if let PostEvent::Published = event.payload { self.notifier.notify(format!("{} published", event.stream)).await?; } Ok(()) } } Rules. It runs after the commit, at least once: make the effect idempotent. No batch: a failed batch is handled again, which a transaction undoes for a read model but not for an e-mail. A reset (reset() on the processors, every instance stopped) rebuilds the read models; these skip what they already handled. A reaction that sends commands to another aggregate root is the same: a namespace holding that root's command port, sending idempotent commands.
documents.s: 28. Side effects are namespaces that do not replay

documents.t: Set with TrackingOptions (.options(..) on the unit, or with_options on a processor), and on the handler for batches: Segments (TrackingOptions::default().segments(8)): the log is split by aggregate, each segment handled in order by the instance that claims it. One aggregate's events stay in order; instances share segments through the token store, and a dead instance's claims expire (Event processing). Batches (batch = 64 on a namespace's handler, or .batch_size(64) for a processor of your own): a worker handles the events already waiting, up to the size, in one unit of work with one token update. It never waits to fill one. A failed batch rolls back and its events are handled one at a time. For handlers whose writes the transaction undoes: the blog's summaries rebuild 5000 events in 0.25 s instead of 4.6 s. Dead letters (events.processor(name, h).with_dead_letters(queue, after)): an event that failed after times is parked with every later event of its aggregate, and the segment moves on; retry_dead_letters() replays each sequence in order once fixed.
documents.s: 29. Scaling a processor: segments, batches, dead letters

documents.t: Shape. The same projection runs inline (InlinePublisher::new(store).with_projection(p), after each commit, in the caller's task) or in tracking processors (Cqrs::new(events).projection(p)); only the composition root changes. Rules. Inline, Tx = (), each namespace sees the commit isolated from the others, and there are no retries, no replays and no subscriptions. A failure never undoes the commit: it goes to the on_failure policy (LogFailures by default). For tests and simple applications.

Problem. Publishing to a broker from a command handler loses messages when the broker is down, or sends ones whose commit failed. Shape. Forward is an event handler that publishes each event through a one-method port (Publish), encoded by a Codec, keyed by its stream. Run it in a tracking processor and the log is the outbox: let outbox = app.events().track("outbox", Forward::new(broker, Json, "posts")); // or a topic per event Forward::routed(broker, Json, |event: &EventEnvelope<PostEvent>| event.event_type.replace('.', "-")); Rules. Nothing is published that was not committed, and nothing committed is lost: at least once, from the processor's token, retried while the broker is down. Outgoing.position is the consumers' deduplication id; the stream key keeps each aggregate in order on a broker that orders by key. Forward does not replay. Fan-out. One Forward per destination, each its own tracking processor with its own token: a broker that is down holds only its own forwarder back. On a broker that fans out (an AMQP fanout exchange), one forwarder and a queue per consuming service do the same. Coming the other way. A Subscribe port (Axon 5's SubscribableEventSource) hands messages, in batches, to a Consumer, and acknowledges a batch once it returned Ok; a failed batch is delivered again. The consumer usually turns each message into a command: impl Consume for OnPostPublished { async fn consume(&self, messages: &[Incoming]) -> Result<(), HandlerError> { for message in messages { let PostEvent::Published { id, title } = message.decode(&Json)?; match self.gateway.send(Notify { post: id, title }).await { Ok(()) | Err(NoticeError::AlreadySent) => {} // delivered twice Err(error) => return Err(error.into()), } } Ok(()) } } Delivery is at least once: deduplicate by Incoming.position, or make the command idempotent (above, the notice is a new stream per post, so a second delivery conflicts). A message that can never be handled is better acknowledged and logged than failed, or it comes back forever. RabbitMQ. examples/bank runs both sides: the bank forwards its accounts' log, a compliance service consumes it into its own commands. cqrs-async-amqp implements both ports over lapin, in the shapes of Watermill's presets, one constructor each: let amqp = Amqp::connect("amqp://127.0.0.1:5672/%2f").await?; // out: a fanout exchange per topic let outbox = events.track("outbox", Forward::new(AmqpPublisher::fanout(&amqp).await?, Json, "posts")); // in, in the notifications service: its own queue, bound to `posts` let subscriber = AmqpSubscriber::fanout(&amqp, "posts", "notifications").await?; subscriber.subscribe(OnPostPublished { gateway }, shutdown).await?; Constructor Publishes to Consumers fanout a fanout exchange named after the topic every bound queue gets every message; a service's instances share its queue queue a durable queue named after the topic compete for its messages topic one topic exchange, the topic as routing key bind by pattern (post.*) Messages are persistent and published with confirms; the event's type, version, position (the message id), stream and metadata travel as properties and headers. A failed batch goes back to the queue after a pause that grows with the failures in a row, or, with dead_letter_failures(), to the queue's dead-letter exchange. Without TLS by default: an amqps:// broker needs the rustls or native-tls feature.

Problem. A read model needs the events of two aggregate roots in the order they happened (a feed showing each post with its author's current name), but each root appends to its own log, of its own event type. Shape. The read side names what it joins: an enum with a variant per log's event type, #[event(fan_in)]. The logs are read as one, in their global order, and the projection is an ordinary one over that enum: // src/application/feed.rs #[derive(Clone, Debug, cqrs::DomainEvent)] #[event(fan_in)] enum FeedEvent { Post(PostEvent), User(UserEvent), } #[cqrs::projection(name = "feed", events = FeedEvent, namespaces("feed"))] struct FeedProjection { /* .. */ } // composition root, PostgreSQL let posts = pg.events::<PostEvent>("posts"); let users = pg.events::<UserEvent>("users"); let feed: PgFanIn<FeedEvent, _> = pg.fan_in((&posts, &users)); let running = feed.projection(FeedProjection { /* .. */ }).spawn(); // in memory: the stores share their numbering let posts = Events::new(InMemoryEventStore::<PostEvent>::new()); let users = Events::new(posts.store().beside::<UserEvent>()); let feed: Events<FeedEvent, _> = Events::fan_in((&posts, &users)); examples/bank projects its customers' portfolios this way. Rules. Only a projection that joins logs has such an enum: no event type joins every log, and the write side does not change (commands keep appending to each root's own log; nothing is appended through the fan-in). The enum takes each event's name, version and tags from the event it wraps, and converts from each (From). Each log is decoded by its own store, upcasters included. The order is the global one: positions come from one sequence for the database (one numbering for in-memory stores made beside each other), so the fan-in's cursor tracks gaps over all its logs at once. The fan-in follows its sources: their commits, and the notifications listen relays to them, wake its processors. Over PostgreSQL each page is one index range per log, merged.

Shape. Around a whole gateway, generic over every message: // src/infrastructure/observability.rs impl<M: Message> Interceptor<M> for Audit { async fn intercept<N, F>(&self, message: M, metadata: Metadata, next: N) -> Result<M::Output, M::Error> where N: FnOnce(M, Metadata) -> F + Send, F: Future<Output = Result<M::Output, M::Error>> + Send, { let correlation_id = metadata.get("correlation_id").cloned(); let result = next(message, metadata).await; // .. record the command, its correlation id, result.is_ok() result } } // src/config.rs: .commands(..).intercept(Audit(Arc::clone(&audit))) Rules. It may change the message or metadata, refuse (return an error without calling next), or inspect the result. To refuse with a typed error, bound it: impl<C: Command> Interceptor<C> for RequireUser where C::Error: From<Unauthorized>. Without the builder: Intercepted::new(gateway, Audit(..)).

Shape. Around an event handler or a projection, inside its unit of work, with its context (Axon's chain.proceed(context)): // src/infrastructure/observability.rs impl<E: DomainEvent, Tx: Send> EventInterceptor<E, Tx> for Measured { async fn intercept<N: EventChain<Tx>>( &self, event: &EventEnvelope<E>, context: &mut ProcessingContext<'_, Tx>, next: N, ) -> Result<(), HandlerError> { let started = Instant::now(); let result = next.proceed(context).await; // .. count and time it, trace a failure result } } // src/config.rs: .projection(Intercepted::new(projection, Measured(Arc::clone(&metrics)))) Rules. What it writes in context.transaction() commits or rolls back with the handler; one that writes names its Tx, others stay generic. Not calling next skips the event (it counts as handled). proceed consumes the chain: the handler runs at most once per attempt. Chains are tuples, nested statically: an interceptor that only calls next costs about nothing (Performance).

// src/application/queries/post_summary.rs pub trait PostSummaryRepository: Send + Sync { // what queries read fn find(&self, id: PostId) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Option<PostSummary>, StoreError>> + Send; fn published(&self) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Vec<PostSummary>, StoreError>> + Send; } pub trait PostSummaryStore<Tx>: Send + Sync { // what the projection writes, in its unit of work fn save(&self, tx: &mut Tx, summary: PostSummary) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), StoreError>> + Send; fn update(&self, tx: &mut Tx, id: PostId, change: impl FnOnce(&mut PostSummary) + Send) -> impl Future<Output = Result<bool, StoreError>> + Send; // clear(tx), before a replay } Rules. update with a closure is Axon's managed entity: change in place, no find-clone-save. In the tokens' database, each change commits with its token. Keep it apart from the write side's repository: they differ in storage and consistency.
documents.s: 35. The read model is a port, read and written apart

documents.t: Problem. A client wants a query's result, then each change, and expects to see its own command right away. Shape. The projection lists the queries it refreshes (updates(..), pattern 27); a namespace emits in updated, on every instance, once it handled the event: // src/application/projections/post/summaries.rs async fn updated(&self, event: &EventEnvelope<PostEvent>, updates: &QueryUpdateEmitter<Self>) { let Ok(id) = post_of(event) else { return }; if let Ok(Some(summary)) = self.summaries.find(id).await { updates.emit(|query: &FindPost| query.id == id, Some(summary)); } // .. and ListPublished when the post was published } // src/presentation/graphql/subscription.rs let updates = ctx.data_unchecked::<A>().queries().subscribe(query); // current result, then updates Rules. The channel is picked by the query's type: emitting a query the projection does not list does not compile. The current result is read once the read-model namespaces handled what was committed when the subscription started, so a client sees its own command. Equal consecutive results are not repeated. The client subscribes to the shape it queries: no event-to-API conversion.

Shape. EventFeed<E>::subscribe(after): every committed event after a position, exactly once, in order, then live. Events implements it; the API names the port (type Events: EventFeed<PostEvent>). // src/presentation/graphql/subscription.rs let events = ctx.data_unchecked::<A>().events().subscribe(after); Rules. The stream does not borrow the feed (use<Self, E>), so it can be returned from a resolver or moved into a task. Reconnecting with the last position seen misses nothing. A long-running process with state of its own is a projection with a read model, or a task over this feed.
documents.s: 37. The event feed is a port

documents.t: // tests/domain.rs AggregateFixture::<Post>::creating(ID, |events| Post::create(ID, " Hello ", events)) .expect_events([created()]) .expect_state(|post| assert_eq!(post.title(), "Hello")); AggregateFixture::<Post>::new(ID) .given([created(), PostEvent::Published]) .when(|post, events| post.publish(events)) .expect_error(PostError::AlreadyPublished) .expect_no_events(); No store, no async: past events in, new events or an error out. creating runs a static creation, which has no past.

cqrs::testing::block_on runs a future on the current thread; with the inline wiring (blog::in_memory()), command → projection → query flows are synchronous and deterministic. Tracking processors need Tokio: #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] makes retries' backoff take no time.

A guarantee enforced by types is proven by code that must not compile: /// ```compile_fail,E0277 /// let (blog, _, _) = blog::in_memory(); /// let _ = blog.commands().send(FindPost { id: PostId(1) }); // a query sent as a command /// ``` The blog's lib.rs keeps one per guarantee (a decision assigning state, &mut to a loaded aggregate, a command no gateway handles, a listed command without its handler, a query listed by a command gateway, a command listed twice); the library's are in its rustdoc and crates/cqrs/tests/ui.

Problem. Wiring by hand means building the events, the gateways over them, a processor per namespace, the subscriptions over their progress, and naming every resulting type; switching stores touches all of it. Shape. Cqrs::new(events); each step takes a value and changes the builder's type: // src/config.rs let projection = PostProjection::new(Arc::clone(&summaries), Arc::clone(&notifier)); let app = Cqrs::new(Events::new(store.clone())) .commands(|events| PostCommandGateway::new(posts_over(&store), events)) .intercept(Audit(Arc::clone(&audit))) .queries(PostQueryGateway::new(Arc::clone(&summaries))) .projection(Intercepted::new(projection, Measured(Arc::clone(&metrics)))) .build(); app.commands().send(CreatePost { title }).await?; app.queries().subscribe(FindPost { id }); app.settled().await; // every processor caught up app.stop().await; Rules. The infrastructure is the argument. Events::new(store) in memory, Postgres::new(pool).events::<PostEvent>("posts") on PostgreSQL (one database's store, tokens and transactions; a log per root). The blog's start changes only that and the repository. The unit is the gateway's unit of work. .commands(|events| ..) hands the closure the events for its #[gateway(unit)] field. Synchronous, without a runtime: Cqrs::from_publisher(InlinePublisher::new(store).with_projection(p)). Order is typed. .projection needs events; one that names PgTransaction is accepted only over PostgreSQL. A unit is one root with one projection; several roots are a tuple of units. Nothing is boxed: sending through app.commands() costs what sending through the gateway does. Return the unit by its traits: Cqrs<impl PostCommands, impl PostQueries>. .options(..) applies to the processors started after it; a processor configured beyond them (dead letters, an outbox) is started from app.events() and stopped by its owner.
documents.s: 41. The CQRS unit: a typed builder

documents.t: benchmarks/versus runs the same bank on this library and on cqrs-es 0.5 with postgres-es 0.5, against the same PostgreSQL: open, deposit, withdraw and transfer, one aggregate per account, a balance read model, and a transfer policy crediting the target account. The business rules live in one shared module (bank.rs); each library only wraps them, wired the way its docs recommend. Here, the read model and the transfers are tracking processors with 8 segments and batches of up to 100 events (CQRS_VERSUS_BATCH, default 100); in cqrs-es they run inline after each commit. CQRS_POSTGRES_URL=postgres://cqrs:cqrs@127.0.0.1:55432/cqrs cargo run --release -p cqrs-versus -- 3 32 clients and a 32-connection pool per system, a fresh schema per system, the median of the runs.

The run after Phase 10 (docs/benchmarks/gate-log.md, "after Phase 10"): three rounds, median of the rounds, alternating with the code of the release gate under the same load. Absolute values are ours; the ratio is ours divided by cqrs-es's, with the threshold the gate holds it to. Measure Ours Ours / cqrs-es Gate passes if open account 4086 cmd/s 1.20 ≥ 1.10 mixed load (1k accounts) 3716 cmd/s 1.30 ≥ 1.25 mixed load, p99 17.7 ms 0.69 ≤ 0.76 mixed load: done, read model and transfers included 5500 ms 0.78 ≤ 0.77 hot account (32 writers, one aggregate) 153 cmd/s 1.52 ≥ 1.00 hot account, p99 977 ms 0.50 read model rebuild 40431 events/s 24.9 ≥ 16 5000-event aggregate, full replay, p50 2.84 ms 0.48 ≤ 0.95 5000-event aggregate, snapshot every 100, p50 1.23 ms 0.62 ≤ 0.61 events or money lost by the read model 0 0 The machine was busier than at the release gate (load 4.3-4.9). Two measures miss their threshold by 0.01: the time to done, which the release's code missed by more under the same load (0.86), and the snapshot p50, whose rounds spread from 0.41 to 0.62. Against that code, nothing regressed. At the release gate, on a quieter machine, every measure passed (open account 1.14, mixed 1.35, p99 0.70, done 0.76, hot account 1.44, rebuild 25.5, replay 0.49, snapshot 0.50). cqrs-es's read model loses events in every run (about 170 in each): concurrent commands on one account race in its inline view updates.

Three A/B runs decide the current state, all in gate-log.md: After the command's unit of work, the gateways as handlers and the query updates in the projection (head 768ac7d against 5437e6e, the code before those changes). Head and base are equal within the spread of their own rounds on every measure: the redesign costs nothing measurable on PostgreSQL. Mixed p99 missed its threshold on both codes by the same amount (0.80 and 0.81). PostgreSQL path optimizations (against 263f8cd), four changes, none to the semantics: a conflict returns the stream's version in the append's own statement (no second read); the batch and its metadata are serialized straight to JSON text (no serde_json::Value); an aggregate is rebuilt through LoadStream::replay, which reads and decodes only what rebuilding uses; a page read probes the index only for the positions the page does not hold. Replay p50 went from 4.23 to 2.47 ms (-42%), mixed p99 from 18.6 to 15.1 ms (-19%), hot account from 131 to 158 cmd/s (+21%); those three do not overlap between the two sets of rounds. Before the first release (c315a04 against the optimized code): the public modules, the envelope without per-event copies, the wake-up between instances in the readers' loop and the packaging changed nothing measurable; every gate measure passes.

The rule is not to fall behind cqrs-es. The gate runs at the end of each phase of work, and after any commit that introduces dyn or touches the append path: CQRS_POSTGRES_URL=postgres://cqrs:cqrs@127.0.0.1:55432/cqrs cargo run --release -p cqrs-versus -- 3 cargo bench -p cqrs-benchmarks --bench micro The thresholds are in the table above. To compare two versions of the code, one run of each is not enough: build both release binaries and run them alternately (base, head, base, head, base, head) under the same load, then compare the medians and whether the rounds overlap. The micro-benchmarks are informative: a regression there needs an explanation in the commit, but the table decides.

All numbers come from one laptop (Apple M4 Pro, 14 cores) with PostgreSQL 17 in Docker on the same machine, so the benchmark's 32 clients per system, both libraries and the database share the CPU. What that means for reading them: Load moves everything. Load average was 6.7–12.5 during the latest run (the "after" rounds started under slightly more load) and 10–13 during the A/B before it, mostly the benchmark itself. Earlier, with other processes running (load 10–22), the same binary moved between 2700 and 4500 cmd/s on open account, and the measures that failed changed from one run to the next with the code unchanged. Ratios move with cqrs-es's noise too. A ratio can drop because cqrs-es had a fast run, not because ours was slow. Treat single-run differences under about 20% as noise; trust only A/B rounds that do not overlap. Measures on their limit. The snapshot replay sits exactly on its threshold (0.61) in the latest run, as it did in the baseline: a run landing slightly above needs a second run before it is called a regression. The mixed p99 threshold comes from a ratio (0.63) this machine did not reproduce, with any code, until the PostgreSQL optimizations. A quiet machine is the only absolute gate. The thresholds were written for one; on a loaded one, use the A/B method.

Writes. One statement per append; positions from a sequence, so appends never wait for each other; locks only where the domain overlaps (Storage § Locks). Static dispatch adds nothing measurable on top of the database round trips. Replays.
