LoadStream::replay reads only the sequence, type, version and payload, and decodes each row as it arrives; events are stored as json and decoded straight into their type unless an upcaster applies (Storage § Upcasting). Correctness of the read model. cqrs-es updates views inline, after the commit, with a separate read-modify-write per view: concurrent commands on the same account race and lose updates. Here the projection runs in a tracking processor, each event once, in order per aggregate, in a transaction with its token. Rebuild and catching up. One shared reader per processor routes events to 8 segments in parallel, and each segment handles what is waiting in batches of up to 100, one commit per batch. Measured on the same build (benchmarks/results/versus.md), batches took the time until everything is done from 9287 to 4870 ms, and a rebuild from 6050 to 41420 events/s.

benchmarks/benches/micro.rs (divan): single operations, in memory, no runtime. cargo bench -p cqrs-benchmarks --bench micro cargo bench -p cqrs-benchmarks --bench micro -- interceptors Benchmark What it measures Median unit/command_gateway a command through its gateway and its unit of work 29.4 ns persistence/command_cycle load a 10-event aggregate, decide, commit, in memory 1.02 µs interceptors/command_plain a query through its gateway 3.4 ns interceptors/command_intercepted_4 the same through four pass-through interceptors 13.6 ns (gate-log.md, run of 768ac7d.) Since commands always run in a unit of work, dispatch/* and interceptors/command_* route a query (Echo), to keep measuring the routing alone. unit/command_gateway was 14.3 ns before the command's unit of work: the 15 ns more are its begin, append, commit, announce and retry loop, against a command of about 1 ms on PostgreSQL. An interceptor chain compiles to nested calls: one that does nothing costs nothing measurable; four cost about 3 ns each. What an interceptor does is what it costs. The event benchmarks (interceptors/event_plain, event_intercepted, event_measured: the blog's projection, alone, through a pass-through interceptor, through Measured) were last recorded in docs/benchmarks/baseline.md (16, 11.5 and 50 ns); the other benchmarks (aggregate, loading with and without snapshots, reading a page of the log) are listed there too.

Projections: write in the unit of work's transaction, and update rows in place instead of find-clone-save. Do not check sequences in projections: the processor already delivers each aggregate's events once and in order. Give the namespaces that write a read model a batch (batch = 64 on the handler): one commit per batch of waiting events instead of one per event. Keep side effects at 1. Raise segments for read models with many aggregates; it is fixed by the first instance that initializes the processor's tokens. Snapshot aggregates with long streams (with_snapshots(store, 100)). Keep side effects in their own namespace, so a slow external call never holds the read model back.

The event store is the source of truth. It is not one trait but four, one per capability (cqrs::store), so a component asks only for what it uses and a store for another database implements what that database can do: Port Methods Used by LoadStream<E> load(stream, after), replay(stream, after, apply) rebuilding an aggregate (AggregateLoader) AppendEvents<E, Tx = ()> append, append_if (provided); append_tagged (implemented) the command's unit of work, EventPublishers SourceEvents<E> source(criteria) decisions read by criteria (CommandContext::source), aggregates built from tags ReadLog<E> read_all(after, limit), last_position(), read(cursor, limit), cursor_at(position) tracking processors, subscriptions EventStore<E> is all four at once, implemented for every type that has them: what the in-memory and the PostgreSQL stores offer. Every stored event comes back in an EventEnvelope<E>: stream StreamId: aggregate type and id (post-42) sequence its place in the stream, from 1, gapless position its place in the global log, increasing (not necessarily gapless) event_type, event_version its name and shape version (#[event(name, version)]) recorded_at, metadata when, and what the command was sent with (correlation id, user...) payload the event

load returns the envelopes of a stream after a sequence. replay hands each event (with its sequence) to a closure and returns how many there were: what rebuilding an aggregate needs, and all it needs. By default it goes through load; the PostgreSQL store reads only the sequence, type, version and payload, and decodes each row as it arrives (no metadata, no stream ids, no list of envelopes). With the other optimizations of the same change, that took the median replay of a 5000-event aggregate from 4.23 to 2.47 ms (Performance).

append(tx, stream, expected, events, metadata) stores events atomically per stream, checking an ExpectedVersion: NoStream (creating an aggregate), Exact(n) (the version it was loaded at) or Any. append_if(.., condition) also checks an AppendCondition (Axon 5's dynamic consistency boundary): no event matching its criteria after the position the decision read at. The check and the write are atomic. A store only implements append_tagged: writing the events with their tags, atomically with both checks, and returning what it Recorded (position, sequence, time) for each. The provided methods resolve the tags, build the envelopes, and let an empty append succeed at once, without checking anything. Tx is the transaction the append joins. () means none: the store appends on its own. A database store also appends in a transaction its caller owns (the PostgreSQL store implements AppendEvents<E, sqlx::Transaction<'_, Postgres>>), which is how a command's unit of work commits its events with the repository's writes. Then nothing is visible, nor announced, before that transaction commits. Errors are StoreError::Conflict { stream, expected, actual }, StoreError::ConditionFailed (both a lost race: is_conflict(), decide again on fresh state) or StoreError::Backend(..), which keeps the original error as its source.

read(cursor, limit) returns a LogPage: the events the cursor has not seen (those filling its gaps, then those after it), the Horizon the store knew when it answered, and missing, the positions skipped that nothing was committed at (None: the store cannot tell, so every skipped position may still be filled). The defaults suit a gapless store; a store whose appends commit out of order implements read and cursor_at to report gaps.

InMemoryEventStore<E>: every event in a Vec behind one lock, gapless positions, tags indexed in memory. It is a handle: clones share the same events, so the repository, the unit of work and the processors each hold one. store.all() returns every envelope in order (tests). It appends only on its own (Tx = ()): memory has nothing to roll back. InMemorySnapshots<A>, InMemoryTokenStore and InMemoryDeadLetters complete the set. Everything in memory is lost together when the process ends, which is why the tokens and the read model stay consistent.

cqrs-postgres (MSRV 1.94, the one of sqlx 0.9) keeps everything over a plain sqlx pool. Postgres is the infrastructure every aggregate root of an application shares on one database: the pool, the token store and the transactions. Each root gets its own log: let pg = cqrs_postgres::Postgres::new(pool); pg.migrate().await?; // or MIGRATIONS, in your tool let posts = Cqrs::new(pg.events::<PostEvent>("posts")) // one log per aggregate root .commands(..).projection(..).build(); let users = Cqrs::new(pg.events::<UserEvent>("users")).build(); pg.events(log) is a PgEvents<E>: by hand, Events::new(PostgresEventStore::new(pool, "posts")).with_tokens(PostgresTokenStore::new(pool)).with_transactions(PostgresTransactions::new(pool)). Events need Serialize + DeserializeOwned. Every process sharing the database shares the logs, the tokens and the claims. The crate re-exports its sqlx (cqrs_postgres::sqlx): PgPool and PgTransaction are part of its API.

The schema is crates/cqrs-postgres/migrations/0001_cqrs.sql, idempotent. Two ways to run it: The crate runs it: pg.migrate() (or cqrs_postgres::migrate(&pool)) runs it in one implicit transaction behind an advisory lock, so instances starting together run it one after the other. Your migration tool runs it: cqrs_postgres::MIGRATIONS is the list of (name, statements), for sqlx migrate, sea-orm-migration, refinery... It then owns when they run. The blog runs it as one of its SeaORM migrations: // src/infrastructure/postgres/migration.rs #[async_trait::async_trait] impl MigrationTrait for EventTables { async fn up(&self, manager: &SchemaManager) -> Result<(), DbErr> { for (_, statements) in cqrs_postgres::MIGRATIONS { manager.get_connection().execute_unprepared(statements).await?; } Ok(()) } } The tables keep their names (every statement of the crate is checked against them at compile time). To keep them apart from the application's, run the migrations and the stores in a schema of their own, chosen by the connection's search_path (PgConnectOptions::options([("search_path", "events")])). Table cqrs_events one row per event: log, position (PK), stream type and id, sequence (unique per stream in a log), event type and version, payload and metadata (json: stored as written, returned as is), recorded_at cqrs_event_tags (log, tag, position) the tag index criteria read through cqrs_snapshots newest snapshot per stream, with its revision cqrs_tokens (processor, segment) position, gaps and their horizons, owner, claim expiry, replay bound cqrs_dead_letters (processor, sequence, position) parked events: which event, and why; the event is read back from the log sequence cqrs_position global positions functions cqrs_positions, cqrs_lock position assignment, domain-derived locks

A store reads and appends one named log, the second argument of PostgresEventStore::new(pool, "posts"). One event enum per aggregate root means one log per root, so several roots share a database: let posts = PostgresEventStore::<PostEvent>::new(pool.clone(), "posts"); let users = PostgresEventStore::<UserEvent>::new(pool.clone(), "users"); Each store sees only its log: read_all, read, source, last_position, conditions and lock keys are all per log, and the same stream may exist in two logs. Two stores given the same name share their events, so they must have the same event type. Tokens are per processor name, snapshots per aggregate type.

Positions come from one sequence for the whole database: the logs share one global order, as Axon 5's single event stream does, and a reader following several logs (a fan-in) can rely on it. A sequence per log was considered and dropped: it loses that order. Appends run in parallel, so a transaction that took position 10 can commit after the one that took 11. A reader that saw 11 and remembers only "11" would skip 10 forever. Readers therefore track a Cursor (cqrs::store::Cursor): the highest position seen, and the positions below it not seen yet (Gap { position, horizon }). Each read returns the gaps' events if they appeared, then the events after the cursor. A gap is given up only once nobody can fill it. Each append takes a transaction id before its positions (cqrs_positions), and each read reports its snapshot (xmin, xmax, as a Horizon): a gap seen in a snapshot can only be filled by a transaction older than its xmax, so once the oldest running transaction is newer, the gap is closed. Axon gives a gap up after a timeout, which can lose a slow transaction's event; this cannot. With one sequence for several logs, the positions another log takes are missing from this log's rows. They are not gaps: a page read also returns LogPage::missing, the positions up to the last event read that no log committed in that snapshot, and only those become gaps. The rest are passed over at once. Without it, a processor's cursor carried a hundred gaps or more with two logs under load. (Strategy B, gapless positions with a finalizer as in Axon's PostgreSQL engine, would replace it only if it measured at least as fast.) cursor_at(position) does the same for a reader starting from a position (looking back at most 10 000 positions). Every reader of the global log uses cursors: tracking processors (stored in cqrs_tokens with their gaps), subscriptions, emitters of query updates. cursor.covers(p) means the event at p was seen.

Consistency is per piece of the domain, not per database: every append takes shared advisory locks on keys derived from its events: each tag (from a #[tag] field), each event type, the stream; source(criteria) and a conditional append take the criterion's keys exclusively. So unconditional appends never wait for each other; a conditional append waits only for appends under way that touch what it read, and holds off new ones until it commits, so later ones take positions above the head the decision was read at. Two decisions on different courses run in parallel; two on the same course take turns. Keys are taken in sorted order, so they never deadlock. In the caller's transaction, a conflict aborts the transaction, as any failed statement does in PostgreSQL: the command's unit of work rolls it back and runs the handler again. A condition's locks are held until the transaction ends, so keep a transaction with a conditional append short.

Every statement in the crate is a sqlx::query!, checked against the migrations at build time: columns, parameter and result types, nullability. The check uses the database in CQRS_POSTGRES_URL (set in the crate's sqlx.toml, never an application's DATABASE_URL), or the committed .sqlx/ cache when it is not set, which is the default for builds. After changing a statement, with the migrations applied: cargo sqlx prepare -- -p cqrs-async-postgres

serde is the contract: the adapters that persist ask for Serialize + DeserializeOwned, and the PostgreSQL store writes JSON through serde_json directly. A Codec<T> (encode, decode) is only needed where an adapter stores or sends bytes in a format that is not serde's, such as protobuf, whose binary encoding needs field numbers serde's data model does not carry. Forward, which publishes events to a broker, takes one. Codec Feature For Json json any Serialize + DeserializeOwned Protobuf protobuf any prost::Message your own implement Codec<T> for the types it encodes

Stored events are never rewritten. When an event's shape changes: bump its version: #[event(name = "post.created", version = 2)]; register an upcaster from the old version: use cqrs::store::upcast; use serde_json::json; let store = PostgresEventStore::<PostEvent>::new(pool, "posts").with_upcasters(( upcast("post.created", 1, |payload| payload["Created"]["tags"] = json!([])), upcast("post.created", 2, |payload| payload["Created"]["draft"] = json!(true)), )); Each upcast(type, from, fn) takes the JSON of one type at one version to the next; a tuple (up to 8) chains them, oldest step first. On read, the store asks the chain whether any step applies to the event's type and version (Upcaster::applies, a comparison of a name and an integer): none applies (every event at its current version, the usual case): the stored text is decoded straight into the event type, with no intermediate document; some apply: the text is parsed into a serde_json::Value (StoredEvent), each matching step rewrites it, then it is decoded. So upcasting costs nothing for current events. Upcasters are the core's json feature (StoredEvent, Upcaster, Upcast, upcast in cqrs::store, also re-exported by cqrs-postgres), shared by any store that keeps JSON.

A SnapshotStore<A> keeps aggregate states so a load replays only the events after them. AggregateLoader::with_snapshots(snapshots, every) saves one whenever a load had to replay every events or more; commits never snapshot. The blog's event-sourced repository passes it through: // src/config.rs fn posts_over(store: &PostStore) -> EventSourcedPostRepository<PostStore, InMemorySnapshots<Post>> { EventSourcedPostRepository::new(store.clone()).with_snapshots(InMemorySnapshots::default(), SNAPSHOT_EVERY) } PostgresSnapshotStore::<Post>::new(pool) keeps the newest one per stream in cqrs_snapshots, as JSON, at revision 1. with_revision(n) stamps them: a snapshot of another revision is ignored (the aggregate is replayed, then snapshotted again), so bump it when the aggregate's serialized shape changes. A snapshot that fails to decode is only a full replay. Snapshots are never the truth: deleting them only makes loads slower. () is the snapshot store that keeps none.

Implement the ports your database supports: LoadStream (load; replay if it can read less than an envelope), AppendEvents (append_tagged, for () and for your transaction type if the database has one), SourceEvents (source) and ReadLog (read_all, last_position; plus read and cursor_at if positions can commit out of order). Keep the version check, the condition check and the write atomic. The behavior every store must share is in the core's tests (dcb.rs, stateful.rs): run them against yours.

A unit of work is one transaction: what a command decides, or what a processor does with an event, commits as a whole or not at all. There are two, one at each end of the log: the command's: the gateway opens it, the handler and its repositories write in it, the library appends the recorded events in it and commits; the processor's: a tracking processor opens it, the event handler writes its read model in it, the processor stores its token in it and commits. In both, the library commits, never the handler (as in Axon). The application still owns the transaction's type: it comes from its TransactionManager (() in memory, PgTransaction on PostgreSQL, or its own).

A command gateway (#[cqrs::command_gateway]) sends each command to cqrs::command::dispatch_command, which runs one unit of work through the gateway's #[gateway(unit)] field (a UnitOfWork): begin unit.begin() -> Tx (() without a transaction) handle handler.handle(&command, &mut ctx, &mut tx) repositories read and write in tx; the domain appends to ctx; ctx.record(entity) append append_writes(unit, &mut tx, ctx.take_writes()) what was recorded, entity by entity commit unit.commit(tx) announce unit.announce(events) processors, subscriptions, inline handlers An error at any step before the commit drops tx, which rolls back whatever the handler and its repositories wrote. The events are announced only once committed, so nothing downstream ever sees a rolled-back event. The handler decides and records; it never appends nor commits. ctx.record(entity) assigns the events appended since the last call to that entity and returns the entity evolved by them, at the version they take it to. It is pure: nothing is written yet. A repository that keeps state saves that value, in tx: // src/application/commands/publish_post.rs #[cqrs::command_handler] impl<R: PostRepository, P> CommandHandler<PublishPost> for PostCommandGateway<R, P> { async fn handle( &self, command: &PublishPost, ctx: &mut CommandContext<PostEvent>, tx: &mut R::Tx, ) -> Result<(), BlogError> { let post = self.posts.find(command.id, tx).await?.ok_or(NotFound(command.id))?; post.publish(ctx)?; let post = ctx.record(post); self.posts.save(&post, tx).await?; Ok(()) } } Events appended but never recorded when handle returns Ok are a bug (a forgotten record): debug builds panic.

#[cqrs::command_handler] reads the mode from handle's arguments: handle takes Mode (CommandHandler::Unit) What commits (&self, command, ctx) Autocommit the store appends the recorded events on its own, in one statement. One entity per command. The fastest path, for an event-sourced repository. (&self, command, ctx, tx: &mut Tx) InTransaction<Tx> the unit opens a transaction of its TransactionManager; the handler's writes, the repositories' writes and the events commit together. The blog's handlers take tx: &mut R::Tx, so the repository adapter picks the transaction: EventSourcedPostRepository has Tx = () (its events are its state, save writes nothing), SeaOrmPostRepository has Tx = PgTransaction (each post's row is saved with its events). Two units of work are provided: Unit (#[gateway(unit)]) Autocommit InTransaction<Tx> Events<E, S, C, M> the store appends, then broadcasts Tx = M::Tx: a transaction of its TransactionManager M; the store appends in it (S: AppendEvents<E, M::Tx>) InlinePublisher<E, S, ..> the store appends, then the inline handlers run Tx = () only: memory has no transaction to roll back Cqrs::new(events).commands(|events| PostCommandGateway::new(repo, events)) hands the gateway its unit. On PostgreSQL, cqrs_postgres::Postgres::new(pool).events::<PostEvent>("posts") gives an Events whose transactions are PostgresTransactions (Tx = PgTransaction).
documents.s: Two modes, chosen by the signature

documents.t: If the append finds that the decision was made on stale state, the unit is rolled back and the handler runs again, with a fresh context and a fresh transaction, on fresh state. A lost race is StoreError::ConditionFailed (a DCB condition failed) or a StoreError::Conflict on a stream expected at an exact version. Creating what already exists (a New entity whose stream is there) is not a lost race: running again would fail the same way, so it reaches the caller. CommandHandler::conflict_retries says how many times (8 by default); a handler overrides it in its impl: // crates/cqrs-postgres/tests/postgres.rs /// Decided on a stale copy, it would be decided again: refuse instead. fn conflict_retries(&self) -> u32 { 0 } Since the handler may run more than once, it must have no side effects besides what it writes in tx. An e-mail, a call to another service, a message to a broker: those go to a projection namespace with const REPLAY: bool = false, which runs once the events are committed (see Event processing). The command is taken by reference (&C) for the same reason. The ROLLS_BACK rule. Running the handler again is only safe if nothing it appended survived. UnitOfWork::ROLLS_BACK says whether dropping the transaction undoes the appends: true for a database (TransactionManager::ROLLS_BACK, default true), false in memory (() and InlinePublisher). When a unit that cannot roll back loses a race after recording more than one entity (the first append may have gone through), the handler is not run again: the conflict reaches the caller, and nothing is appended twice. With one entity, nothing was appended when it lost, so it is retried as usual.
documents.s: A lost race runs the handler again

documents.t: Autocommit: recording more than one entity is an error, returned before anything is appended: their appends would be separate statements, not atomic. Take the unit's transaction instead. InTransaction<Tx> on a database: the writes are appended one after the other in the same transaction, so they commit together. Each later write's condition skips the events the run itself just appended (they match what it read), and checks only what others appended. InTransaction<()> in memory: appended one after the other, with no rollback (see the ROLLS_BACK rule). A rule spanning several aggregates may also be one entity built from tags (a dynamic consistency boundary), or a projection namespace reacting to the first aggregate's event. The PostgreSQL test state_and_events_commit_and_roll_back_together checks the transactional mode end to end: a handler failing after it saved its state leaves neither state nor events; one that succeeds leaves both, and its events reach subscribers; a stale version conflicts and undoes the state written with it.

Command interceptors (Interceptor<M>, chained with Intercepted::new(gateway, (A, B)) or the builder's .intercept(..)) run around the gateway's dispatch: once per command, outside its unit of work and outside the retries. They see the command and its metadata, and the final result.

dispatch_command(&handler, command, metadata, &unit) is what a gateway does, and what a test calls to run a handler without one. Outside a command (an import, a test seeding a store), EventPublisher::commit(entity, Pending::new(events)) appends to one entity's stream and announces, with no handler involved.

For each event, a tracking processor runs one unit of work: begin TransactionManager::begin() -> Tx interceptors EventInterceptor::intercept(event, &mut context, next) (outer to inner) handle EventHandler::handle(event, &mut ProcessingContext<'_, Tx>) store token TokenStore::store(&mut tx, token) only if this instance still holds the segment commit TransactionManager::commit(tx) committed EventHandler::committed(event) after the commit only Axon phase Here pre-invocation / invocation begin, interceptors, handle prepare commit storing the token in the same transaction commit commit(tx) after commit committed(event) on error / rollback dropping tx (an Err anywhere before the commit) With a batch size above 1 (batch = N on a namespace's handler, or TrackingOptions::batch_size), the events already waiting for a segment share one unit of work: begin → [interceptors → handle] e1 … eN → store the token (past eN) → commit → committed e1 … eN Each event still gets its own ProcessingContext (with its own replay flag) over the same transaction. If any of them fails, the whole batch rolls back and its events are handled again one unit of work each, so the failing one is retried, or parked, on its own. crates/cqrs/tests/unit_of_work.rs records every phase with an in-memory transactional store and checks this order, including a failed attempt that leaves nothing behind and a failed batch handled again one by one.

The TransactionManager (cqrs::processing), and only it: begin hands a transaction out, commit consumes it. The token store, the dead-letter queue and the event handler borrow it (&mut Tx), so none of them can commit it, keep it or choose its type. pub trait TransactionManager: Send + Sync { type Tx: Send; const ROLLS_BACK: bool = true; fn begin(&self) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Self::Tx, StoreError>> + Send; fn commit(&self, tx: Self::Tx) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), StoreError>> + Send; } Transaction manager Tx What a rollback undoes () () nothing: in memory, a crash loses read model and tokens together cqrs_postgres::PostgresTransactions PgTransaction (sqlx::Transaction<'static, Postgres>) the handler's SQL, the interceptors' SQL, the token move, the dead letter your own anything Send whatever your commit makes durable The processor checks at compile time that everything takes part in the same transaction: TokenStore<Tx = M::Tx>, DeadLetterQueue<E, M::Tx> and EventHandler<E, M::Tx>. A read model written in a database transaction cannot be run with tokens kept in memory, nor dead letters kept in memory with tokens in a database. Events::new(store).with_tokens(tokens).with_transactions(transactions) sets both; cqrs_postgres::Postgres::events does it for PostgreSQL.

A handler reaches the transaction through its context. The blog's summaries namespace is generic over it, and its repository writes in it: // src/application/projections/post/summaries.rs #[cqrs::event_handler(namespace = "summaries", batch = 64)] impl<S, N, Tx> EventHandler for PostProjection<S, N> where S: PostSummaryRepository + PostSummaryStore<Tx>, N: Send + Sync, Tx: Send, { async fn handle( &self, event: &EventEnvelope<PostEvent>, context: &mut ProcessingContext<'_, Tx>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerError> { let tx = context.transaction(); let found = match &event.payload { PostEvent::Created { id, title } => { let summary = PostSummary { id: *id, title: title.clone(), published: false, }; self.summaries.save(tx, summary).await?; true } // ... }; // ... Ok(()) } } The read model must live where the transaction reaches: a PostgreSQL projection keeps its tables in the database of the token store. A handler that writes elsewhere (memory, another service) still runs in the unit of work, but its writes are not rolled back with it: make them idempotent.
documents.s: Writing the read model in the unit

documents.t: Atomic. The handler's writes (in Tx), the interceptors' writes and the processor's new position commit together or not at all. Exactly once into the read model for writes in Tx: a crash before the commit loses the writes and the position together, so the event is handled again; after it, both are there. At least once for everything else: writes outside Tx and side effects in handle may happen again on a retry. After commit only: committed runs once the commit succeeded, never for a rolled-back attempt. It cannot fail, and a crash between the commit and committed skips it. Ownership. TokenStore::store moves the token only if this instance still holds the segment's claim. If another instance took it over, it returns false: the unit is rolled back and the worker stops, so two instances never both commit the same event. Order. Events of one aggregate are handled one at a time, in order; a failing event holds its segment back (or is parked). Batches change nothing above. A batch commits all its events and the token past the last one, or none of them.

Failure. An Err from an interceptor or the handler drops the transaction and the processor retries the event in a new unit of work, with exponential backoff. With dead letters, after the configured number of attempts the event is parked, in the unit of work that moves the token past it. Reset. reset() moves the tokens back, then runs the handler's reset in a unit of work of its own (a PostgreSQL projection truncates its tables there). During the replay, context.replay() is true for the events stored before the reset, and handlers with const REPLAY: bool = false never see them (nor do their interceptors). Dead-letter retries. retry_dead_letters() runs each parked event in a unit of work like the processor's: handle, the letter's removal, commit, committed. The removal commits with what the handler wrote, so neither a crash nor two retries running at once apply a parked event twice. See Event processing for the settings.

impl<'a, Tx> ProcessingContext<'a, Tx> { pub fn new(transaction: &'a mut Tx, replay: bool) -> Self; pub fn in_processor(transaction: &'a mut Tx, replay: bool, processor: &'a str) -> Self; pub fn transaction(&mut self) -> &mut Tx; // the unit of work pub fn replay(&self) -> bool; // Axon's ReplayStatus pub fn processor(&self) -> &str; // "post.summaries"; "" outside a processor } The processor builds it; handlers and interceptors receive &mut to it. Tests build one directly (ProcessingContext::new(&mut (), false)) to call a handler without a processor.

Event interceptors (EventInterceptor<E, Tx>) receive the handler's context and call the rest of the chain with it, so what they write in context.transaction() commits or rolls back with the handler's changes: impl EventInterceptor<ClockEvent, PgTransaction> for AuditRows { async fn intercept<N: EventChain<PgTransaction>>( &self, event: &EventEnvelope<ClockEvent>, context: &mut ProcessingContext<'_, PgTransaction>, next: N, ) -> Result<(), HandlerError> { sqlx::query("INSERT INTO clock_audit (position) VALUES ($1)") .bind(i64::try_from(event.position).unwrap()) .execute(&mut **context.transaction()) .await?; next.proceed(context).await } } The PostgreSQL test a_failing_projection_interceptor_rolls_the_write_back runs a failing interceptor and AuditRows around a projection: the failed attempt's audit row and total are both rolled back, and the retry writes each once.

An InlinePublisher runs its handlers in the caller's task, after the command's unit committed. There is no transaction to share (Tx = ()): the append was the commit. Each event goes through handle, then committed; a failure stops that handler for the rest of the commit and goes to the publisher's OnFailure policy. No retries, no tokens.

The transaction both units hand out on PostgreSQL is sqlx's (PgTransaction), the one the library's stores append and move tokens in. cqrs_sea_orm::SeaOrm is a borrowed view of it that SeaORM's query builders run on, so a repository or a read model written with SeaORM commits with the events or with the token: // src/infrastructure/postgres/post_summaries.rs impl PostSummaryStore<PgTransaction> for SeaOrmPostSummaries { async fn save(&self, tx: &mut PgTransaction, summary: PostSummary) -> Result<(), StoreError> { let row = post_summary::ActiveModel { id: Set(key(summary.id)?), title: Set(summary.title), published: Set(summary.published), }; post_summary::Entity::insert(row) .exec(&SeaOrm::new(tx)) .await .map_err(backend)?; Ok(()) } // ... } SeaOrm::new(tx) borrows the transaction: it can neither commit it nor outlive it. The other way round does not work: SeaORM's DatabaseTransaction keeps its connection private and does not lend it, and the library's statements are sqlx's, checked at compile time.

Axon 5 Here Why Resources on the context (putResource, getResource by key) The context carries one typed resource, Tx; anything else is a field of the handler or interceptor A heterogeneous resource map needs dyn Any. A custom TransactionManager can make Tx any struct (a transaction plus a tenant, a clock...). Lifecycle callbacks registered at runtime (onCommit, runOnAfterCommit, onError) Fixed hooks: committed after commit; rollback on Err; interceptors around handle Registered closures need boxing. Every component that needs a phase implements it statically. One ProcessingContext type for commands, queries and events CommandContext<E> for commands, ProcessingContext<Tx> for events, none for queries Each carries exactly what its handlers use, typed. The command's transaction from the context tx: &mut Tx as an argument of handle The mode (Autocommit or InTransaction<Tx>) is part of the handler's type, so a unit that cannot provide that transaction does not compile.

To keep read models (or a command's state) in another database, implement TransactionManager for something that opens its transactions: begin opens a transaction on the database the read models live in; commit commits it; dropping it without a commit must roll it back; ROLLS_BACK stays true unless dropping it undoes nothing. Then a TokenStore with the same Tx, whose store updates the token in that transaction only if the owner still holds the segment's claim (returning false otherwise), and, for dead letters, a DeadLetterQueue<E, Tx>. Events::new(store).with_tokens(your_tokens) .with_transactions(your_transactions) runs every processor in your units of work; handlers name ProcessingContext<'_, YourTx> (or stay generic).

This guide builds a small blogging backend, one layer at a time: posts are drafted, retitled and published; readers query summaries and subscribe to changes; publishing notifies someone. By the end it runs on PostgreSQL behind a GraphQL API, with tracking processors, live queries and interceptors. The finished code is examples/blog; every snippet here comes from it. Part You build You learn 1. The domain Post, its events and rules, domain tests aggregates, decisions with an appender, events and tags, the test fixture 2. Commands CreatePost, RetitlePost, PublishPost, the repository port, the command gateway the gateway as the handler, CommandContext and record, units of work, retries 3. Queries and the read model PostSummary, its ports, FindPost, ListPublished, the query gateway the read side as ports, the query gateway 4. The projection PostProjection and its summaries namespace, the first working app event handlers, inline processing, the composition root 5. Going asynchronous tracking processors, a notifications namespace Events, units of work, replay, segments 6. Live Queries and Subscriptions subscriptions to FindPost and ListPublished query update emitters, reading your own writes 7. Interceptors an audit log, projection metrics dispatch and event interceptors 8. PostgreSQL the same app on a database, with SeaORM the Postgres stores, one transaction for state and events, transactional projections 9. The API GraphQL over axum, event subscriptions ports for the presentation layer, metadata, the event feed Prerequisites: Rust 1.89+ (edition 2024) for cqrs; the blog itself needs 1.94, because SeaORM 2 does. For part 8, a PostgreSQL (docker run -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=cqrs -p 55432:5432 postgres:17). The project layout we end up with: src/ ├── domain/ # Post, PostEvent, PostError, PostId ├── application/ │ ├── commands/ # one file per command and its handler, the repository port, the command gateway │ ├── queries/ # one file per query and its handler, the read model and its ports, the query gateway │ └── projections/ # PostProjection: one namespace per file (summaries, notifications) ├── infrastructure/ # adapters: repositories, read model, notifier, interceptors, postgres/ ├── presentation/ # GraphQL + axum, against a ports trait ├── config.rs # the composition root: the blog's Cqrs unit └── lib.rs # modules and re-exports Side effects, such as the notification, are not a folder of their own: they are a namespace of the projection that does not replay (part 5).

The last layer exposes the application over HTTP: GraphQL queries and mutations through the gateways, and subscriptions through the subscription queries and the event feed. Like the application, it is written against ports only: the traits the gateways and the projection generate.

// src/presentation/mod.rs use cqrs::{Cqrs, store::EventFeed}; pub trait BlogApi: Send + Sync + 'static { /// Sends the commands. type Commands: PostCommands; /// Answers the queries, and streams their results as they change. type Queries: PostQueries + PostSubscriptions; /// Streams the committed events (the framework's port: no feed to write). type Events: EventFeed<PostEvent>; fn commands(&self) -> &Self::Commands; fn queries(&self) -> &Self::Queries; fn events(&self) -> &Self::Events; } Each bound comes from a macro argument met earlier: PostCommands, from #[cqrs::command_gateway(commands = PostCommands, ..)]: CommandGateway<CreatePost> + CommandGateway<RetitlePost> + CommandGateway<PublishPost>. PostQueries, from #[cqrs::query_gateway(queries = PostQueries, ..)]: a QueryGateway for each query. PostSubscriptions, from #[cqrs::projection(.., subscriptions = PostSubscriptions)]: subscribing to each query in the projection's updates(..). EventFeed<PostEvent>, the library's port on the committed events. The bounds are the contract: the API compiles against any application that sends these commands, answers and streams these queries, and streams these events. No resolver knows the store, the repository or the read model. Any CQRS unit that exposes those ports is the API, whatever its gateways, interceptors and stores: // src/presentation/mod.rs impl<C, Q, E> BlogApi for Cqrs<C, Q, E> where C: PostCommands + 'static, Q: PostQueries + PostSubscriptions + 'static, E: EventFeed<PostEvent> + 'static, { type Commands = C; type Queries = Q; type Events = E; fn commands(&self) -> &C { Cqrs::commands(self) } fn queries(&self) -> &Q { Cqrs::queries(self) } fn events(&self) -> &E { Cqrs::events(self) } } A second impl forwards Arc<A>, which is what the server shares. So the in-memory start_in_memory() and the PostgreSQL start(pool) serve the same API, unchanged, and a test double needs only these ports.
documents.s: One trait for everything the API needs

documents.t: // src/presentation/graphql/mutation.rs pub struct MutationRoot<A>(PhantomData<fn() -> A>); #[Object(name = "Mutation")] impl<A: BlogApi> MutationRoot<A> { /// Writes a draft and returns its id. async fn create_post(&self, ctx: &Context<'_>, title: String) -> Result<ID> { let api = ctx.data_unchecked::<A>(); let id = api .commands() .send_with(CreatePost { title }, metadata(ctx)) .await .map_err(from_blog)?; Ok(ID(id.to_string())) } /// Makes a draft public. Returns the post's id. async fn publish_post(&self, ctx: &Context<'_>, id: ID) -> Result<ID> { let api = ctx.data_unchecked::<A>(); api.commands() .send_with(PublishPost { id: post_id(&id)? }, metadata(ctx)) .await .map_err(from_blog)?; Ok(id) } // retitle_post: the same, with RetitlePost } /// The metadata of the request being resolved (none outside HTTP). fn metadata(ctx: &Context<'_>) -> Metadata { ctx.data_opt::<Metadata>().cloned().unwrap_or_default() } Each resolver builds the command's own struct and sends it. send_with is generic over the command, and its result is that command's output and error: PostId for CreatePost, () for PublishPost. There is no enum of commands to wrap them in, nor one of outputs to unwrap. The same holds for any other transport. A JSON endpoint or a queue consumer deserializes the command's type (the blog's commands derive serde::Deserialize) and sends it: let command: CreatePost = serde_json::from_slice(&body)?; let id = api.commands().send(command).await?; A transport that takes several commands on one route chooses the type from its own envelope (a field, a topic, a path) and deserializes into it. The HTTP layer turns a header into metadata, so every event a request causes stores its correlation id (and the Audit interceptor of part 7 records it): // src/presentation/http.rs pub const CORRELATION_HEADER: &str = "x-correlation-id"; async fn execute<A: BlogApi>( State(schema): State<BlogSchema<A>>, headers: HeaderMap, request: GraphQLRequest, ) -> GraphQLResponse { let mut metadata = Metadata::new(); if let Some(id) = headers.get(CORRELATION_HEADER).and_then(|value| value.to_str().ok()) { metadata.insert("correlation_id".to_owned(), id.to_owned()); } schema.execute(request.into_inner().data(metadata)).await.into() } BlogError maps to GraphQL errors by variant, never by parsing messages: an extension code of DOMAIN_RULE, NOT_FOUND or CONFLICT (retry), and a generic INTERNAL error for Store, whose details stay in the logs.
documents.s: Mutations send commands, with the request's metadata

documents.t: Two kinds, both plain Streams handed to async-graphql: // src/presentation/graphql/subscription.rs #[Subscription(name = "Subscription")] impl<A: BlogApi> SubscriptionRoot<A> { /// The post now (`null` if it does not exist yet), then again each time /// it changes. Same shape as `Query.post`. async fn post(&self, ctx: &Context<'_>, id: ID) -> Result<impl Stream<Item = Result<Option<PostNode>>> + use<A>> { let query = FindPost { id: post_id(&id)? }; let updates = ctx.data_unchecked::<A>().queries().subscribe(query); Ok(updates.map(|post| post.map(|post| post.map(PostNode::from)).map_err(from_blog))) } /// The id of each post published from now on. async fn post_published(&self, ctx: &Context<'_>) -> Result<impl Stream<Item = Result<ID>> + use<A>> { let events = ctx.data_unchecked::<A>().events(); let now = events.last_position().await.map_err(from_store)?; Ok(events.subscribe(now).filter_map(|event| { ready(match event { Ok(event) => { matches!(event.payload, PostEvent::Published).then(|| Ok(ID(event.stream.id().to_owned()))) } Err(error) => Some(Err(from_store(error))), }) })) } // published_posts: subscribe(ListPublished); post_events(after, postId, kinds) } Subscription queries (post, publishedPosts) have the same shape as the queries: what most clients want. queries().subscribe(FindPost { id }) yields the current result, then each update the projection's summaries namespace emits in updated (part 6). The current result waits until the read model handled what was committed when the subscription started, so a client that subscribes right after its mutation sees it. On PostgreSQL, a client gets the updates on whichever instance it is connected to. The event log (postEvents(after, postId, kinds), postPublished) streams committed events, filtered on the server with StreamExt / TryStreamExt combinators (where NestJS would pipe RxJS operators). subscribe(after) delivers every event after a position exactly once, in order: a client reconnecting with the last position it saw misses nothing. The streams do not borrow the API (+ use<A>), so async-graphql can hold them for the lifetime of the WebSocket.

// src/presentation/http.rs pub fn router<A: BlogApi>(schema: BlogSchema<A>) -> Router { Router::new() .route(GRAPHQL_PATH, get(graphiql).post(execute::<A>)) .route_service(SUBSCRIPTIONS_PATH, GraphQLSubscription::new(schema.clone())) .route("/health", get(|| async { "ok" })) .with_state(schema) } main picks the wiring, and serves either the same way: // src/main.rs match std::env::var("BLOG_DATABASE_URL") { Ok(url) => serve(blog::start(PgPool::connect(&url).await?).await?).await, Err(_) => serve(blog::start_in_memory()).await, } /// Serves `running` until Ctrl-C, then stops its processors. async fn serve<C, Q, R, E>(running: Running<C, Q, R, E>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> where Arc<cqrs::Cqrs<C, Q, E>>: BlogApi, { let schema = graphql::schema(Arc::clone(&running.app)); // ... --schema prints the SDL and returns let address = std::env::var("BLOG_ADDR").unwrap_or_else(|_| "127.0.0.1:8000".to_owned()); let listener = TcpListener::bind(&address).await?; axum::serve(listener, http::router(schema)) .with_graceful_shutdown(async { let _ = tokio::signal::ctrl_c().await; }) .await?; running.stop().await; // processors finish their current event Ok(()) } serve only asks that the unit be a BlogApi: the presentation layer does not know which wiring it got. cargo run -p blog # in memory; GraphiQL on http://127.0.0.1:8000/graphql BLOG_DATABASE_URL=postgres://... cargo run -p blog # on PostgreSQL, with SeaORM cargo run -p blog -- --schema # prints the SDL

tests/api.rs runs against start_in_memory(): most tests execute against the schema directly, and a few drive the real router, mutations over HTTP and subscriptions over a WebSocket (graphql-transport-ws). One checks what the interceptors recorded: // tests/api.rs #[tokio::test] async fn interceptors_audit_every_command_and_measure_the_projection() { let (running, schema) = app(); // ... `server` serves http::router(schema) on a local port; createPost with // "x-correlation-id: req-9", then publishPost twice (the second refused) ... running.settled().await; let entries = running.audit.entries(); let summary: Vec<_> = entries .iter() .map(|e| (e.command, e.correlation_id.as_deref(), e.succeeded)) .collect(); assert_eq!( summary, [ ("CreatePost", Some("req-9"), true), ("PublishPost", None, true), ("PublishPost", None, false) ] ); assert_eq!( running.metrics.handled(), 4, "created and published, each applied once in each of the projection's two namespaces" ); server.abort(); running.stop().await; }
Patterns: every pattern used in this guide, with its rules. Unit of work: what commits when, and the guarantees. Event processing and Storage: the operational reference.

Inline processing makes every command wait for every handler, and loses a failed handler's work. A real application commits the command and returns; the read model and the notifications follow on their own, each tracking how far it got, retrying what fails, and never applying an event twice. That is a tracking processor.

The asynchronous unit starts from the post events, Events, which it builds everything else on: // src/config.rs pub fn start_in_memory() -> Running<impl PostCommands, impl PostQueries + PostSubscriptions, InMemoryPostSummaryRepository, PostEvents> { let store = PostStore::default(); let summaries = Arc::new(InMemoryPostSummaryRepository::default()); let notifier = Arc::new(InMemoryNotifier::default()); // ...the audit log and the metrics of part 7 let projection = PostProjection::new(Arc::clone(&summaries), Arc::clone(&notifier)); let app = Cqrs::new(Events::new(store.clone())) .commands(|events| PostCommandGateway::new(posts_over(&store), events)) .queries(PostQueryGateway::new(Arc::clone(&summaries))) .projection(projection) .build(); // ... } (The real function also wraps the gateway and the projection in interceptors: part 7.) Events::new(store) is everything asynchronous about the post events: the store, a live broadcast of what is committed, and where the processors keep their positions and the transactions they run in (in memory and none, by default; part 8 gets all of them from PostgreSQL with Postgres::new(pool).events::<PostEvent>("posts")). Cloning it is cheap and shares all of it. The events are also the publisher. A command's unit of work appends to the store, commits, then broadcasts. .commands(|events| ..) hands them to the closure that builds the gateway, as in part 4. The repository and the gateways are the same as in part 4; only what the unit starts from changed. .projection(p) starts a TrackingProcessor per namespace, named after it: "post.summaries" and "post.notifications", each with its own token.
documents.s: From the events to the unit

documents.t: A processor: reads the store from its stored position (its token), then follows the live broadcast, falling back to the store whenever it misses something; runs events in a unit of work: begin, handle, store the token, commit, then committed. The summaries take up to 64 waiting events per unit of work (their batch = 64); the notifications one; on failure, rolls back and retries with backoff, holding back only the failing post's segment. The namespaces are independent: a notifier outage does not hold the summaries back, and each catches up from its own token once things work again.

With the in-memory token store, the unit of work is (): there is no transaction, so "handled" and "token stored" are two steps, and a crash loses both together (the read model is in memory too). With PostgreSQL (part 8) the unit of work is a real transaction, and the summaries are written in it with the token: each event applies exactly once. A side effect outside the transaction (the notification) is at least once. See Unit of work for the full contract.

Commands now return before the projection ran. PostEvents names the unit's events: // src/config.rs pub type PostEvents = Events<PostEvent, PostStore>; pub struct Running<C, Q, R, E> { pub app: Arc<Cqrs<C, Q, E>>, pub summaries: Arc<R>, pub notifier: Arc<InMemoryNotifier>, pub audit: Arc<AuditLog>, pub metrics: Arc<ProjectionMetrics>, } The unit knows its processors: app.settled() waits until every one of them handled every event committed so far, and app.stop() stops them, each after its current event. Running forwards both. use blog::application::{commands::{CreatePost, PublishPost}, queries::PostSummaryRepository}; use cqrs::command::CommandGateway; #[tokio::test] async fn the_read_model_follows_the_commands() { let running = blog::start_in_memory(); let id = running.app.commands().send(CreatePost { title: "Async".into() }).await.unwrap(); running.app.commands().send(PublishPost { id }).await.unwrap(); running.settled().await; assert!(running.summaries.find(id).await.unwrap().unwrap().published); assert_eq!(running.notifier.sent(), ["post-1 published"]); running.stop().await; } An application with several aggregate roots has a unit per root; a tuple of units waits and stops together: (posts, users).settled().await (cqrs::Units). Part 6 removes most of this waiting: subscription queries wait for the read model themselves.

To rebuild the summaries from scratch (a bug fixed in the projection, a new column), stop the processors, reset the projection, and start it again: let events = running.app.events().clone(); let (summaries, notifier) = (Arc::clone(&running.summaries), Arc::clone(&running.notifier)); running.stop().await; // every processor of the unit let projection = PostProjection::new(summaries, notifier); events.projection(projection).reset().await?; // tokens back to 0, then `reset`: clear() // then build the unit again over `events`: the summaries replay Resetting moves every namespace's tokens back to the start and calls each handler's reset. The events stored so far are then a replay (context.replay() is true): summaries sees them, and rebuilds; notifications has REPLAY = false, so it skips them: nobody is notified twice. It picks up again with the first new event. Resetting fails with ResetError::Running while any instance still runs the processors.

Cqrs::new(Events::new(store.clone())) // ... .options(TrackingOptions::default().segments(8)) .projection(projection) // ... .options applies to the processors started after it. The log is split into 8 segments by post: posts are projected in parallel, each post's events in order. TrackingOptions::default().batch_size(n) sets the batch of every namespace that does not set its own; batch = 64 on the summaries wins over it. A batch never waits to fill: a worker takes what is already queued for its segment, so it adds no latency under light load. With a shared token store (PostgreSQL), several instances of the application split the segments between them and take over a dead instance's segments when its claims expire. See Event processing.

A failing event is retried with exponential backoff (retry_initial, retry_max in TrackingOptions), holding back only its segment; the other namespace and the other segments go on. By default the namespaces of a projection retry for as long as it takes, which is what a read model needs: skipping an event would leave it wrong. A side effect may rather park an event its target keeps refusing, so the rest goes on. Give the projection a dead-letter queue when it is wired: let parked = InMemoryDeadLetters::default(); // PostgresDeadLetters on PostgreSQL let app = Cqrs::new(Events::new(store.clone())) // ... .projection_with(projection, |processors| processors.with_dead_letters(parked.clone(), 5)) .build(); After five failed attempts the event is parked, under its namespace's processor ("post.notifications"), with the later events of the same post behind it, so a post's order is kept; other posts flow. Once the cause is fixed, events.projection(..).with_dead_letters(parked, 5).retry_dead_letters() handles them, namespace by namespace. See Event processing. Next: 6. Live Queries and Subscriptions.

A command is an intent to change state. Each one gets its own file, with its message and its handler. The handlers are methods of one struct, the command gateway, which holds what they share: the application's repository, and the unit of work they run in. A handler finds the post, lets the domain decide, and records what it decided; the unit of work appends the events and commits once the handler returns.

The application says how its handlers find and keep posts. It is a port, with only what the use cases need: // src/application/commands/post_repository.rs use std::future::Future; use cqrs::{aggregate::Loaded, store::StoreError}; use crate::domain::{Post, PostId}; pub trait PostRepository: Send + Sync { /// The unit of work's transaction it works in. type Tx: Send; /// An id no post has yet. fn next_id(&self, tx: &mut Self::Tx) -> impl Future<Output = Result<PostId, StoreError>> + Send; /// The post, at the version it was read at; `None` if it does not /// exist. fn find( &self, id: PostId, tx: &mut Self::Tx, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Option<Loaded<Post>>, StoreError>> + Send; /// Keeps `post` as the command left it (after its recorded events, at /// their version), in `tx`. fn save(&self, post: &Loaded<Post>, tx: &mut Self::Tx) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), StoreError>> + Send; } Loaded<Post> is the post plus the version it was read at, which the append checks. It derefs to &Post only: nobody can change the post through it, only through events. Tx is the transaction of the command's unit of work, lent to the repository. Whatever the repository writes in it commits together with the post's events, or not at all. Each adapter picks its own. The blog has two adapters. In memory, a post is rebuilt from its events with the library's AggregateLoader. Its events are its state, so saving writes nothing more, and there is no transaction (Tx = ()): // src/infrastructure/event_sourced_post_repository.rs impl<S, N> PostRepository for EventSourcedPostRepository<S, N> where S: LoadStream<PostEvent> + SourceEvents<PostEvent>, N: SnapshotStore<Post>, { type Tx = (); async fn next_id(&self, (): &mut ()) -> Result<PostId, StoreError> { Ok(PostId(self.next_id.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed))) } async fn find(&self, id: PostId, (): &mut ()) -> Result<Option<Loaded<Post>>, StoreError> { self.loader.load(&id).await } async fn save(&self, _: &Loaded<Post>, (): &mut ()) -> Result<(), StoreError> { Ok(()) } } On PostgreSQL (part 8), SeaOrmPostRepository keeps each post's state in a table, with SeaORM, in the same transaction the events are appended in (Tx = PgTransaction). The handlers never know which one they got. A finder that is not by id (posts by slug, by author) belongs in a read model (part 3): the event store finds aggregates by id only.

Every use case fails the same way, classified by origin, so an API maps it without parsing strings: // src/application/error.rs use cqrs::{aggregate::NotFound, store::StoreError}; use crate::domain::{PostError, PostId}; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq)] pub enum BlogError { /// The domain refused (a 4xx). Domain(PostError), /// No post has this id (a 404). NotFound(PostId), /// Someone else changed the post in between: retry. Conflict, /// Storage failed (a 5xx). Store(String), } impl From<PostError> for BlogError { fn from(error: PostError) -> Self { Self::Domain(error) } } impl From<NotFound<PostId>> for BlogError { fn from(NotFound(id): NotFound<PostId>) -> Self { Self::NotFound(id) } } impl From<StoreError> for BlogError { fn from(error: StoreError) -> Self { match error { StoreError::Conflict { .. } | StoreError::ConditionFailed => Self::Conflict, // `StoreError` may gain variants: anything else is the store's. other => Self::Store(other.to_string()), } } } From<StoreError> is required: the unit of work's own failures (an append that conflicts, a commit that fails) reach the caller as the command's error.

// src/application/commands/mod.rs #[cqrs::command_gateway(commands = PostCommands, handles(CreatePost, RetitlePost, PublishPost))] pub struct PostCommandGateway<R, P> { /// Where posts are found and kept. posts: R, /// The unit of work every command runs in: it opens the transaction /// the handlers and the repository write in, appends what they /// recorded, and commits. #[gateway(unit)] events: P, } impl<R, P> PostCommandGateway<R, P> { pub fn new(posts: R, events: P) -> Self { Self { posts, events } } } The gateway is the handler: one struct per side, with one CommandHandler<C> impl per command, in that command's file. The handlers share the struct's fields, so there is no struct per handler and no Arc to pass the repository around. handles(..) is the list of commands it routes, each to its impl, decided at compile time. A command listed without its impl does not compile, where the gateway is declared; so does a query listed as a command. #[gateway(unit)] marks the field the commands run in: a UnitOfWork, which the composition root provides (part 4). P stays generic here. commands = PostCommands also generates a trait, CommandGateway<CreatePost> + CommandGateway<RetitlePost> + CommandGateway<PublishPost>, implemented by whatever routes the three: this gateway, the gateway behind interceptors (part 7), a test double. Code that sends commands names impl PostCommands, not the gateway.

// src/application/commands/retitle_post.rs use cqrs::{ aggregate::NotFound, command::{CommandContext, CommandHandler}, }; use crate::{ application::{ BlogError, commands::{PostCommandGateway, PostRepository}, }, domain::{PostEvent, PostId}, }; /// Changes the title of a draft. #[cqrs::command(error = BlogError)] #[derive(Debug, serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize)] pub struct RetitlePost { pub id: PostId, pub title: String, } /// Loads the post, lets the domain rename it and saves the result; nothing /// is committed if the domain refuses. #[cqrs::command_handler] impl<R: PostRepository, P> CommandHandler<RetitlePost> for PostCommandGateway<R, P> { async fn handle( &self, command: &RetitlePost, ctx: &mut CommandContext<PostEvent>, tx: &mut R::Tx, ) -> Result<(), BlogError> { let post = self.posts.find(command.id, tx).await?.ok_or(NotFound(command.id))?; post.retitle(command.title.as_str(), ctx)?; let post = ctx.record(post); self.posts.save(&post, tx).await?; Ok(()) } } What each piece does: The message owns its result type. #[cqrs::command(output = T, error = E)] makes the struct a Command whose send returns Result<T, E>; output defaults to (). Whoever sends RetitlePost gets Result<(), BlogError> without knowing the handler. CommandContext is the command's context (Axon 5's EventAppender with its processing context): the events the domain appends, and the command's metadata, which every event carries. It is an EventAppender<PostEvent>, so the domain takes it as &mut impl EventAppender<PostEvent> and never sees the rest. A fresh one per run. find, decide, record, save. ctx.record(post) assigns the events appended so far to that post, and returns the post evolved by them, at their version. It is pure: nothing is written yet. The repository saves that post in tx (the event-sourced one does nothing; the SeaORM one writes the row). The handler never commits. Once handle returns Ok, the unit of work appends what was recorded, expecting the version the post was read at, and commits. If handle returns an error, nothing is appended and the transaction is rolled back. Events appended but never recorded are a bug (a forgotten record): debug builds panic. The command is borrowed (&RetitlePost), because the handler may run more than once (below). #[cqrs::command_handler] reads the event type and the unit of work from the signature, and marks the gateway as handling the command, for handles(..). By hand: impl<R: PostRepository, P> CommandHandler<RetitlePost> for PostCommandGateway<R, P> where PostCommandGateway<R, P>: Send + Sync, { type Event = PostEvent; type Unit = InTransaction<R::Tx>; // `Autocommit` without a `tx` argument async fn handle(&self, command: &RetitlePost, ctx: &mut CommandContext<PostEvent>, tx: &mut R::Tx) -> Result<(), BlogError> { .. } } // For the gateway that lists `RetitlePost`. impl<R, P> Handles<RetitlePost> for PostCommandGateway<R, P> {} PublishPost is the same, with post.publish(ctx).

Creating has nothing to find. The repository hands out an id, the domain decides without a post (Post::create is an associated function), and the events are recorded for New::<Post>(id), which expects the post's stream not to exist: // src/application/commands/create_post.rs /// Creates a draft post and returns its id. #[cqrs::command(output = PostId, error = BlogError)] #[derive(Debug, serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize)] pub struct CreatePost { pub title: String, } #[cqrs::command_handler] impl<R: PostRepository, P> CommandHandler<CreatePost> for PostCommandGateway<R, P> { async fn handle( &self, command: &CreatePost, ctx: &mut CommandContext<PostEvent>, tx: &mut R::Tx, ) -> Result<PostId, BlogError> { let id = self.posts.next_id(tx).await?; Post::create(id, command.title.as_str(), ctx)?; let post = ctx.record(New::<Post>(id)); self.posts.save(&post, tx).await?; Ok(id) } } If two creations got the same id, the second append fails with a conflict: a post is never overwritten. A command that creates its aggregate when it is missing (a counter that starts at zero) decides on the state before any event, and records to whichever it got: self.counters.find(id).await?.unwrap_or_else(|| New(id).into()).

The handler's signature chooses how its unit of work runs: Without a tx argument (handle(&self, command, ctx)), the mode is Autocommit: what the handler recorded is appended by the store in one statement. The fastest path, for one entity per command. Recording a second entity is an error: their appends would not be atomic. With tx: &mut Tx, the mode is InTransaction<Tx>: the unit opens the transaction, the handler and its repository write in it, the recorded events are appended in it last, and the unit commits. Everything commits together, or nothing does. The blog's handlers take tx: &mut R::Tx, because the repository works in a transaction: () in memory, a PgTransaction on PostgreSQL. The same handler code runs on both. Who runs the unit is the gateway's #[gateway(unit)] field: an InlinePublisher (in memory, the projections run right after each commit), or Events (asynchronous, with the transactions of its TransactionManager). Both are wired in part 4 and 5.

The append expects the post at the version it was read at. If someone appended to it in between, the unit is rolled back and the handler runs again, with a fresh context and transaction, on fresh state: up to 8 times. After that, the caller gets BlogError::Conflict. A handler changes the number by overriding conflict_retries in its impl (0: never rerun). Two cases are not retried: creating what exists already (a New whose stream exists is not a race that rerunning can win), and a unit that cannot roll back (memory) after more than one write went through, since rerunning would append the first one twice. So a command handler has no side effects besides writing in tx. An email sent from a handler could be sent twice. Side effects belong after the commit, in a namespace of the projection that does not replay (part 5).

A handler is a method of the gateway: you can call it with a context of your own, and nothing is written. To commit, run it in a unit of work with dispatch_command, which is what the gateway does for each command: // tests/flow.rs use cqrs::{ command::{CommandContext, CommandHandler, dispatch_command}, event::Metadata, processing::InlinePublisher, store::InMemoryEventStore, testing::block_on, }; #[test] fn handlers_can_be_called_directly_without_any_bus() { block_on(async { // A handler is a method of the gateway: called with an appender, it // decides and records, and nothing is written. let store = InMemoryEventStore::new(); let gateway = PostCommandGateway::new(EventSourcedPostRepository::new(store.clone()), ()); let mut events = CommandContext::new(); let id = gateway .handle(&CreatePost { title: "direct".into() }, &mut events, &mut ()) .await .unwrap(); assert_eq!((id, events.writes().len()), (PostId(1), 1)); // In a unit of work of the caller's: it commits (the repository // handed out id 1 already, to the run above). let unit = InlinePublisher::new(store); let id = dispatch_command(&gateway, CreatePost { title: "direct".into() }, Metadata::new(), &unit) .await .unwrap(); assert_eq!(id, PostId(2)); assert_eq!( dispatch_command(&gateway, PublishPost { id }, Metadata::new(), &unit).await, Ok(()) ); }); } block_on comes with the library: these tests need no async runtime. Through the gateway, it is send. Code that sends commands depends on the commands it sends, not on the gateway: // tests/flow.rs pub async fn create_and_publish<G>(gateway: &G, title: &str) -> Result<PostId, BlogError> where G: CommandGateway<CreatePost> + CommandGateway<PublishPost>, { let id = gateway.send(CreatePost { title: title.to_owned() }).await?; gateway.send(PublishPost { id }).await?; Ok(id) } The two commands are not atomic: if publishing fails, the post stays created as a draft. send_with(command, metadata) sends a command with metadata (a correlation id, the user), which every event it causes carries (part 9). Next: 3. Queries and the read model.
The domain is the business rules and nothing else: no store, no bus, no runtime. A post is drafted with a title, may be retitled while it is a draft, and is then published, after which it is frozen.

[package] name = "blog" edition = "2024" [dependencies] cqrs-async = "0.1.0-alpha.1" # `cqrs::` in code; "derive" and "tokio" are on by default serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }

// src/domain/post/id.rs use std::fmt; use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize}; /// Identifies a post. Its `Display` form (`42`) is the suffix of the post's /// event stream (`post-42`), so it must never change for a stored post. #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, PartialOrd, Ord, Serialize, Deserialize)] pub struct PostId(pub u64); impl fmt::Display for PostId { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result { self.0.fmt(f) } } /// Back from the `Display` form (a stream's suffix). impl std::str::FromStr for PostId { type Err = std::num::ParseIntError; fn from_str(text: &str) -> Result<Self, Self::Err> { text.parse().map(Self) } } The FromStr is the way back: a projection reads a post's id from its event with event.aggregate_id::<Post>(), which parses the stream's suffix.

Events are facts, in the past tense, one enum per aggregate (in PostgreSQL, each aggregate's events get a log of their own: part 8): // src/domain/post/event.rs use super::PostId; #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize, cqrs::DomainEvent)] pub enum PostEvent { /// A draft was created. Always the first event of a post's stream. #[event(name = "post.created")] Created { id: PostId, title: String }, /// The draft's title changed. #[event(name = "post.retitled")] Retitled { title: String }, /// The post became public; no event follows it. #[event(name = "post.published")] Published, } DomainEvent gives each variant its stored type name. Name them explicitly: the default is the Rust name, so renaming a variant would break the events already stored. Each variant also has a schema version (#[event(version = 2)], default 1), for upcasting. serde is for stores that serialize (PostgreSQL, part 8). The in-memory store does not need it.

Every event has tags (TagResolver, which every DomainEvent has), and the derive writes them from the fields marked #[tag]: each becomes a tag keyed by the field's name, valued by its Display. A post's events need none: a post is found by its stream, post-42. So the blog marks no field, and its events have no tags. Tags matter when a decision spans more than one stream. This is the library's own test of dynamic consistency boundaries: a subscription counts for a course and for a student, so it is tagged with both: // crates/cqrs/tests/dcb.rs #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, cqrs::DomainEvent)] enum SchoolEvent { #[event(name = "course.opened")] CourseOpened { #[tag] course: u32, capacity: usize, }, #[event(name = "student.subscribed")] Subscribed { #[tag] course: u32, #[tag] student: u32, }, } /// Every event tagged with its id: its opening and its subscriptions. #[cqrs::aggregate(event = SchoolEvent, tag = "course")] struct Course { id: u32, capacity: usize, students: Vec<u32> } tag = "course" builds a Course from every event tagged course=<id>, whichever stream holds it, and its writes are refused if any such event was appended since it was loaded. See Patterns for the details; the blog does not need them.

// src/domain/post/error.rs /// A business rule the post refused to break. Nothing is recorded when an /// operation returns one of these. #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] pub enum PostError { EmptyTitle, SameTitle, AlreadyPublished, PublishedPostsAreFrozen, } // + Display and std::error::Error

// src/domain/post/mod.rs use cqrs::aggregate::EventAppender; use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize}; #[cqrs::aggregate(name = "post", event = PostEvent)] #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)] pub struct Post { id: PostId, title: String, published: bool, } impl Post { /// How an event changes the post, both when it is recorded and when it /// is replayed: no validation, no failure. fn apply(&mut self, event: &PostEvent) { match event { PostEvent::Created { title, .. } | PostEvent::Retitled { title } => { self.title.clone_from(title); } PostEvent::Published => self.published = true, } } /// Drafts the post `id`, unpublished. There is no post yet, so this /// takes none: commit it to `cqrs::aggregate::New`, which expects the /// post's stream not to exist. pub fn create( id: PostId, title: impl Into<String>, events: &mut impl EventAppender<PostEvent>, ) -> Result<(), PostError> { let title = valid_title(title.into())?; events.append(PostEvent::Created { id, title }); Ok(()) } pub fn retitle( &self, title: impl Into<String>, events: &mut impl EventAppender<PostEvent>, ) -> Result<(), PostError> { if self.published { return Err(PostError::PublishedPostsAreFrozen); } let title = valid_title(title.into())?; if title == self.title { return Err(PostError::SameTitle); } events.append(PostEvent::Retitled { title }); Ok(()) } pub fn publish(&self, events: &mut impl EventAppender<PostEvent>) -> Result<(), PostError> { if self.published { return Err(PostError::AlreadyPublished); } events.append(PostEvent::Published); Ok(()) } /// The post as a repository that keeps state stored it (rather than /// rebuilding it from its events). pub fn restore(id: PostId, title: String, published: bool) -> Self { Self { id, title, published } } pub fn title(&self) -> &str { &self.title } pub fn is_published(&self) -> bool { self.published } } fn valid_title(title: String) -> Result<String, PostError> { let title = title.trim(); if title.is_empty() { Err(PostError::EmptyTitle) } else { Ok(title.to_owned()) } } #[cqrs::aggregate] writes the Aggregate impl. You could write it instead: impl cqrs::aggregate::Aggregate for Post { const TYPE: &'static str = "post"; // stream prefix: post-42 type Id = PostId; // the `id` field (or one marked #[aggregate(id)]) type Event = PostEvent; fn initial(id: &PostId) -> Self { // where replay starts: other fields at Default Self { id: id.clone(), title: Default::default(), published: Default::default() } } fn id(&self) -> &PostId { &self.id } fn evolve(&mut self, event: &PostEvent) { Self::apply(self, event) } } The rules this shape enforces: State changes only through events. Decisions take &self; assigning self.published = true in publish does not compile. Creating takes no post. create is an associated function (Axon 5's static creational command handler): there is no post to decide on yet, and none can be created twice by calling it on one that exists. Its events are recorded for New::<Post>(id), which expects the stream not to exist (part 2). initial is only where replay starts. No buffer in the aggregate. Decisions append to the appender they are given (Axon 5's EventAppender); the struct stays plain data, so derives and serde work as usual. A decision sees the state from before it ran. The appended events are applied when they are recorded. The domain barely knows the framework. EventAppender<E> is implemented for every Extend<E>, so a decision could take &mut impl Extend<PostEvent> and the domain would import nothing from cqrs but its macros. restore is for a repository that keeps a post's state in a table instead of rebuilding it from events (part 8). It is not a way around the rules: every change still goes through a decision and its events.

Given past events, when a decision runs, expect events or an error. No store, no async: // tests/domain.rs use blog::domain::{Post, PostError, PostEvent, PostId}; use cqrs::testing::AggregateFixture; const ID: PostId = PostId(7); fn created() -> PostEvent { PostEvent::Created { id: ID, title: "Hello".into() } } #[test] fn creating_a_post_appends_created() { AggregateFixture::<Post>::creating(ID, |events| Post::create(ID, " Hello ", events)) .expect_events([created()]) .expect_state(|post| assert_eq!(post.title(), "Hello")); } #[test] fn a_post_is_published_once() { AggregateFixture::<Post>::new(ID) .given([created(), PostEvent::Published]) .when(|post, events| post.publish(events)) .expect_error(PostError::AlreadyPublished) .expect_no_events(); } #[test] fn a_published_post_is_frozen() { AggregateFixture::<Post>::new(ID) .given([created(), PostEvent::Published]) .when(|post, events| post.retitle("Other", events)) .expect_error(PostError::PublishedPostsAreFrozen); } creating runs a creation on no post; new(..).given(..) replays past events first. Next: 2. Commands.

Logging, metrics, auditing and authorization apply to every message, not to one use case, so they stay out of the handlers. Two kinds of interceptor, as in Axon: dispatch interceptors (Interceptor<M>) around a gateway: every command or query, with its metadata, before and after its handler; handler interceptors (EventInterceptor<E, Tx>) around an event handler or a projection, inside its unit of work, with its processing context. Both wrap with Intercepted::new(inner, interceptors), and a tuple chains several, the first outermost. The blog keeps its two in src/infrastructure/observability.rs.

// src/infrastructure/observability.rs use cqrs::{ Interceptor, Message, event::{DomainEvent, EventEnvelope, Metadata}, processing::{EventChain, EventInterceptor, HandlerError, ProcessingContext}, }; #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] pub struct AuditEntry { pub command: &'static str, pub correlation_id: Option<String>, pub succeeded: bool, } #[derive(Debug, Default)] pub struct AuditLog(Mutex<Vec<AuditEntry>>); /// Records every command the gateway handles, after it is handled. #[derive(Clone)] pub struct Audit(pub Arc<AuditLog>); impl<M: Message> Interceptor<M> for Audit { async fn intercept<N, F>(&self, message: M, metadata: Metadata, next: N) -> Result<M::Output, M::Error> where N: FnOnce(M, Metadata) -> F + Send, F: Future<Output = Result<M::Output, M::Error>> + Send, { let correlation_id = metadata.get("correlation_id").cloned(); let result = next(message, metadata).await; let command = std::any::type_name::<M>().rsplit("::").next().unwrap_or_default(); let entry = AuditEntry { command, correlation_id, succeeded: result.is_ok() }; self.0.0.lock().expect("audit log poisoned").push(entry); result } } One impl, generic over the message, covers every command the gateway routes. The unit wraps its whole command gateway with .intercept: let audit = Arc::new(AuditLog::default()); let app = Cqrs::new(Events::new(store.clone())) .commands(|events| PostCommandGateway::new(posts_over(&store), events)) .intercept(Audit(Arc::clone(&audit))) // Intercepted<PostCommandGateway<..>, Audit> // ... .build(); let mut metadata = Metadata::new(); metadata.insert("correlation_id".to_owned(), "req-1".to_owned()); app.commands().send_with(CreatePost { title: "Audited".into() }, metadata).await?; assert_eq!(audit.entries()[0].correlation_id.as_deref(), Some("req-1")); Intercepted is a gateway: it routes every command the inner gateway handles, so it is still impl PostCommands, and nothing downstream changes. Queries are intercepted the same way, by handing Intercepted::new(PostQueryGateway::new(..), interceptor) to .queries(..).

An interceptor refuses by returning an error without calling next. To return a typed error, it requires the message's error to accept it: use cqrs::{Interceptor, command::Command, event::Metadata}; pub struct Unauthorized; impl From<Unauthorized> for BlogError { fn from(_: Unauthorized) -> Self { BlogError::Store("unauthorized".into()) } // or a dedicated variant } pub struct RequireUser; impl<C: Command> Interceptor<C> for RequireUser where C::Error: From<Unauthorized>, { async fn intercept<N, F>(&self, message: C, metadata: Metadata, next: N) -> Result<C::Output, C::Error> where N: FnOnce(C, Metadata) -> F + Send, F: Future<Output = Result<C::Output, C::Error>> + Send, { if !metadata.contains_key("user") { return Err(Unauthorized.into()); } next(message, metadata).await } } // in the builder: a tuple chains them, the first outermost .intercept((Audit(audit), RequireUser)) Audit is outermost, so refused commands are audited too.
