// src/infrastructure/observability.rs #[derive(Debug, Default)] pub struct ProjectionMetrics { handled: AtomicU64, busy_us: AtomicU64, } /// Counts and times every event handled, and traces the ones that fail. #[derive(Clone)] pub struct Measured(pub Arc<ProjectionMetrics>); impl<E: DomainEvent, Tx: Send> EventInterceptor<E, Tx> for Measured { async fn intercept<N: EventChain<Tx>>( &self, event: &EventEnvelope<E>, context: &mut ProcessingContext<'_, Tx>, next: N, ) -> Result<(), HandlerError> { let started = Instant::now(); let result = next.proceed(context).await; let busy = u64::try_from(started.elapsed().as_micros()).unwrap_or(u64::MAX); self.0.busy_us.fetch_add(busy, Ordering::Relaxed); match &result { Ok(()) => { self.0.handled.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed); } Err(error) => tracing::warn!(position = event.position, %error, "projection failed"), } result } } let projection = PostProjection::new(Arc::clone(&summaries), Arc::clone(&notifier)); // in the builder: .projection(Intercepted::new(projection, Measured(Arc::clone(&metrics)))) next is the rest of the chain (more interceptors, then the handler). next.proceed(context) runs it in the same unit of work; not calling it skips the event, which then counts as handled. Wrapped around the projection, it runs for every namespace: two events (created, published) count 4, each applied once by summaries and once by notifications. Generic over Tx, Measured runs in any unit of work. An interceptor that writes in the transaction names it (part 8 has one). The intercepted projection keeps its namespaces, their REPLAY and their batch; events a namespace skips on replay skip its interceptors too. updated is not intercepted: it is not part of the unit of work. A pass-through interceptor costs nothing measurable; Measured costs its two clock reads (about 50 ns).

// src/config.rs pub fn start_in_memory() -> Running<impl PostCommands, impl PostQueries + PostSubscriptions, InMemoryPostSummaryRepository, PostEvents> { let store = PostStore::default(); let summaries = Arc::new(InMemoryPostSummaryRepository::default()); let notifier = Arc::new(InMemoryNotifier::default()); let audit = Arc::new(AuditLog::default()); let metrics = Arc::new(ProjectionMetrics::default()); let projection = PostProjection::new(Arc::clone(&summaries), Arc::clone(&notifier)); let app = Cqrs::new(Events::new(store.clone())) .commands(|events| PostCommandGateway::new(posts_over(&store), events)) .intercept(Audit(Arc::clone(&audit))) .queries(PostQueryGateway::new(Arc::clone(&summaries))) .projection(Intercepted::new(projection, Measured(Arc::clone(&metrics)))) .build(); Running { app: Arc::new(app), summaries, notifier, audit, metrics, } } The stores and the services are created here; the unit makes the publisher from the events, gives the command gateway its unit of work, starts a processor per namespace, makes the queries subscribable, and infers every type. The ports say what comes out. Next: 8. PostgreSQL.

One mechanism serves two kinds of clients: streamed results of many values: a query whose answer keeps arriving (an SSE stream, a live query that re-renders a list); real-time events: a client told as things happen (a GraphQL subscription, a WebSocket). Both subscribe to the same query a client would ask once: FindPost { id } gives the summary now, then every new version. Axon calls these subscription queries: the query's current result, then the updates the projection emits once it handled each change.

Updates come from the projection that changes the results, so it is the projection that declares them (part 4): // src/application/projections/post/mod.rs #[cqrs::projection( name = "post", events = PostEvent, namespaces("summaries", "notifications"), updates(FindPost, ListPublished), subscriptions = PostSubscriptions )] pub struct PostProjection<S, N> { /* ... */ } updates(FindPost, ListPublished) gives the projection one channel per query. Together they are QueryUpdateEmitter<Self>; the struct gets no new fields. subscriptions = PostSubscriptions generates the trait of whatever can subscribe to all of them: QuerySubscriptions<FindPost> + QuerySubscriptions<ListPublished>. The queries module re-exports it, so callers find it next to PostQueries.

A namespace emits in updated, next to its handle: // src/application/projections/post/summaries.rs #[cqrs::event_handler(namespace = "summaries", batch = 64)] impl<S, N, Tx> EventHandler for PostProjection<S, N> where S: PostSummaryRepository + PostSummaryStore<Tx>, N: Send + Sync, Tx: Send, { // handle and reset: part 4 /// Pushes the summary queries' new results, on every instance, once /// this namespace handled the event (whichever instance did): the /// post's new summary, and the new list of published posts if it /// changed. async fn updated(&self, event: &EventEnvelope<PostEvent>, updates: &QueryUpdateEmitter<Self>) { let Ok(id) = post_of(event) else { return }; if let Ok(Some(summary)) = self.summaries.find(id).await { updates.emit(|query: &FindPost| query.id == id, Some(summary)); } if matches!(event.payload, PostEvent::Published) && let Ok(published) = self.summaries.published().await { updates.emit(|_: &ListPublished| true, published); } } } updates.emit(filter, result) sends result to the subscriptions whose query filter accepts. The type of the filter's argument picks the channel: |query: &FindPost| .. reaches FindPost subscribers, and the result must be FindPost's output. A query missing from updates(..) does not compile. When it runs. updated runs after the namespace committed the event, outside its unit of work, so a subscriber never sees a change that was rolled back. It runs on every instance of the application, once the namespace handled the event, whichever instance did: with several instances sharing the segments, a subscriber connected to any of them sees every change. That is why it is not committed, which runs only on the instance that handled the event. It does not run for replayed events. It reads the read model rather than computing the result from the event: the summary is already up to date, and the query and its updates then cannot disagree.

Nothing else to wire. .projection(..) (part 5) creates the channels, starts one emitter per namespace that has an updated, and makes the unit's queries subscribable to the projection's updates(..). app.queries() still answers plain queries, and now also implements PostSubscriptions, which start_in_memory returns as impl PostQueries + PostSubscriptions. use cqrs::query::QuerySubscriptions; use futures_util::StreamExt; let mut post = std::pin::pin!(running.app.queries().subscribe(FindPost { id })); // a Stream of Result<Option<PostSummary>, BlogError> let now = post.next().await; // the current result let next = post.next().await; // after the next change to this post The first result waits for the read model. It is computed once the namespaces that see replays (the read models: summaries, not notifications) handled every event committed when the subscription started. A client subscribing right after its own command sees it. Equal results are not repeated. The subscription listens before the first result is computed, so no update is lost in between; one equal to the result before it is dropped. A slow subscriber is dropped. One more than 256 updates behind is forgotten: its stream ends, and the client subscribes again. The inline unit of part 4 (in_memory) has no subscriptions: there is no runtime to push from, and updated does not run inline. Part 9 serves these streams as GraphQL subscriptions (post, publishedPosts), each one a subscribe on the unit's queries. Next: 7. Interceptors.

So far the blog keeps everything in memory. On PostgreSQL, the library's stores keep the events and the processors' tokens, and the blog's own infrastructure keeps the rest with SeaORM: each post's state in a table, and the read model. Both write in the library's transactions, so a post's state commits with its events, and a summary with the processor's token. What changes is the composition root and two adapters. The domain, the handlers, the projection and the queries stay as they are: they are written against the ports (PostRepository, PostSummaryRepository, PostSummaryStore<Tx>), and the transaction type is a parameter.

# examples/blog/Cargo.toml [dependencies] cqrs = { workspace = true, features = ["derive", "tokio"] } cqrs-postgres.workspace = true cqrs-sea-orm.workspace = true # SeaORM in the library's transactions sea-orm = { version = "2.0.4", default-features = false, features = ["macros", "sqlx-postgres", "runtime-tokio"] } sea-orm-migration = { version = "2.0.4", default-features = false, features = ["sqlx-postgres", "runtime-tokio"] } cqrs-postgres and cqrs-sea-orm need Rust 1.94 (sqlx 0.9 and SeaORM 2); cqrs itself stays at 1.89. cqrs-postgres re-exports the sqlx it is built on (cqrs_postgres::sqlx::PgPool): use that one to name the pool and PgTransaction. Events are stored as JSON, so PostEvent derives serde since part 1.

let pg = cqrs_postgres::Postgres::new(pool); let events = pg.events::<PostEvent>("posts"); // what Cqrs::new takes Postgres holds what every aggregate root of the application shares on one database: the pool, the token store (PostgresTokenStore) and the transactions (PostgresTransactions). events(log) gives one root its events service (cqrs_postgres::PgEvents<PostEvent>): a store on the log "posts", tokens and units of work in the database. Another root gets another log on the same Postgres. All logs share one sequence of global positions, so a processor can still read them in one order (Storage § Logs). Postgres is a shortcut. By hand, the same is Events::new(PostgresEventStore::new(pool, "posts")).with_tokens(PostgresTokenStore::new(pool)).with_transactions(PostgresTransactions::new(pool)).
documents.s: One database, one log per aggregate root

documents.t: The library ships its schema as SQL (cqrs_postgres::MIGRATIONS), and does not decide when it runs. The blog adds it as the first migration of its own SeaORM migrator, next to its tables: // src/infrastructure/postgres/migration.rs pub struct Migrator; #[async_trait::async_trait] impl MigratorTrait for Migrator { fn migrations() -> Vec<Box<dyn MigrationTrait>> { vec![Box::new(EventTables), Box::new(BlogTables)] } } /// The library's tables: `cqrs_postgres::MIGRATIONS`, as they are. struct EventTables; #[async_trait::async_trait] impl MigrationTrait for EventTables { async fn up(&self, manager: &SchemaManager) -> Result<(), DbErr> { for (_, statements) in cqrs_postgres::MIGRATIONS { manager.get_connection().execute_unprepared(statements).await?; } Ok(()) } } BlogTables creates posts and post_summaries from their SeaORM entities, and the post_ids sequence. An application without a migration tool calls pg.migrate().await? instead: idempotent, behind a lock, so instances starting together take turns.
documents.s: Migrations: the library's tables are one of yours

documents.t: PostRepository has type Tx: the transaction it works in. The event-sourced adapter from part 2 has Tx = (). The SeaORM adapter has Tx = PgTransaction, the command's own: // src/infrastructure/postgres/post_repository.rs impl PostRepository for SeaOrmPostRepository { type Tx = PgTransaction; async fn find(&self, id: PostId, tx: &mut PgTransaction) -> Result<Option<Loaded<Post>>, StoreError> { let key = i64::try_from(id.0).map_err(StoreError::backend)?; let row = post::Entity::find_by_id(key) .one(&SeaOrm::new(tx)) .await .map_err(backend)?; let Some(row) = row else { return Ok(None); }; let version = u64::try_from(row.version).map_err(StoreError::backend)?; Ok(Some(Loaded::at(Post::restore(id, row.title, row.published), version))) } async fn save(&self, post: &Loaded<Post>, tx: &mut PgTransaction) -> Result<(), StoreError> { let row = post::ActiveModel { id: Set(i64::try_from(post.id().0).map_err(StoreError::backend)?), title: Set(post.title().to_owned()), published: Set(post.is_published()), version: Set(post.version().map_or(0, |version| version as i64)), }; let upsert = OnConflict::column(post::Column::Id) .update_columns([post::Column::Title, post::Column::Published, post::Column::Version]) .to_owned(); post::Entity::insert(row) .on_conflict(upsert) .exec(&SeaOrm::new(tx)) .await .map_err(backend)?; Ok(()) } // next_id: SELECT nextval('post_ids'), in the same transaction } SeaOrm::new(tx) (from cqrs-sea-orm) is SeaORM over a borrowed sqlx transaction: every query builder runs on it. It cannot commit the transaction or outlive it. The opposite is not possible: SeaORM's own DatabaseTransaction does not lend its connection, and the library's statements are sqlx's, checked at compile time. The handlers did not change. They take tx: &mut R::Tx, so their unit of work is InTransaction<PgTransaction>: the unit begins the transaction, the handler finds, decides, ctx.record(post) and saves, then the unit appends the recorded events in the same transaction and commits once. State and events commit together, or not at all. Finding a post now reads one row, whatever its history. The row keeps the version of the post's stream, and the unit appends expecting that version, so two concurrent changes still conflict. The loser's transaction rolls back (its row and its events), and the handler runs again on the new state.
documents.s: The post's state, in the command's transaction

documents.t: The projection writes through PostSummaryStore<Tx>, with the Tx the processor hands it in context.transaction(). In memory Tx is (). On PostgreSQL it is the processor's PgTransaction, the one that moves its token: // src/infrastructure/postgres/post_summaries.rs impl PostSummaryStore<PgTransaction> for SeaOrmPostSummaries { async fn save(&self, tx: &mut PgTransaction, summary: PostSummary) -> Result<(), StoreError> { let row = post_summary::ActiveModel { id: Set(key(summary.id)?), title: Set(summary.title), published: Set(summary.published), }; post_summary::Entity::insert(row) .exec(&SeaOrm::new(tx)) .await .map_err(backend)?; Ok(()) } // update: find the row, apply the change, update it; clear: delete every row } For each batch the processor begins a transaction, the summaries namespace writes its rows, the token is stored, and everything commits. A crash before the commit loses the rows and the token together: the events are handled again and applied once. So save can be a plain insert. If a handling fails after writing, the rollback removes the row, and the retry does not hit the primary key. tests/postgres.rs checks exactly that. The queries read the same table from the pool, through PostSummaryRepository, as before.
documents.s: The read model, in the projection's transaction

documents.t: // src/config.rs pub type PgPostEvents = cqrs_postgres::PgEvents<PostEvent>; pub async fn start( pool: PgPool, ) -> Result<Running<impl PostCommands, impl PostQueries + PostSubscriptions, SeaOrmPostSummaries, PgPostEvents>, DbErr> { Migrator::up(&SqlxPostgresConnector::from_sqlx_postgres_pool(pool.clone()), None).await?; let events = cqrs_postgres::Postgres::new(pool.clone()).events::<PostEvent>("posts"); let summaries = Arc::new(SeaOrmPostSummaries::new(pool.clone())); let notifier = Arc::new(InMemoryNotifier::default()); let audit = Arc::new(AuditLog::default()); let metrics = Arc::new(ProjectionMetrics::default()); let projection = PostProjection::new(Arc::clone(&summaries), Arc::clone(&notifier)); let app = Cqrs::new(events) .commands(|events| PostCommandGateway::new(SeaOrmPostRepository, events)) .intercept(Audit(Arc::clone(&audit))) .queries(PostQueryGateway::new(Arc::clone(&summaries))) .projection(Intercepted::new(projection, Measured(Arc::clone(&metrics)))) .build(); Ok(Running { app: Arc::new(app), summaries, notifier, audit, metrics }) } Against start_in_memory (part 7), only the migrations, the events service and the two adapters differ. The projection is the same PostProjection: its summaries handler is generic over Tx, so it accepts the processor's PgTransaction because SeaOrmPostSummaries implements PostSummaryStore<PgTransaction>. Wiring it with an adapter that only takes () would not compile. The notifications namespace names no transaction, and runs in any unit of work.

The PostgreSQL tests are skipped unless CQRS_POSTGRES_URL points at a database; each test makes a schema of its own: docker run -d --name cqrs-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=cqrs -e POSTGRES_USER=cqrs \ -e POSTGRES_DB=cqrs -p 55432:5432 postgres:17-alpine CQRS_POSTGRES_URL=postgres://cqrs:cqrs@127.0.0.1:55432/cqrs cargo test -p blog --test postgres examples/blog/tests/postgres.rs runs the whole blog on the database and restarts it (ids and tokens carry on), checks that a lost race undoes a post's row and its events, that the read model applies each event once even when the handling fails after writing, and that subscribers on two instances both get a change one of them projected. The library's own tests run the same way with cargo test -p cqrs-async-postgres. The server takes its database from BLOG_DATABASE_URL: BLOG_DATABASE_URL=postgres://cqrs:cqrs@127.0.0.1:55432/cqrs cargo run -p blog

Several instances. Run the same binary several times against the same database. Each namespace's processor (post.summaries, post.notifications) shares its segments through cqrs_tokens: each instance claims some, renews its claims, and takes over a dead instance's segments once its claims expire (claim_timeout, 5 s by default). Set them with .options(TrackingOptions::default().segments(4)) on the builder; the first instance to start a processor fixes its segment count (Event processing § Segments). Commits across instances. An instance's live feed carries only its own commits; without help, the others' reach its processors and subscriptions at their next poll (1 s by default). start(pool) relays them: // src/config.rs let pg = cqrs_postgres::Postgres::new(pool.clone()); let events = pg.events::<PostEvent>("posts"); let listening = pg.listen(&events).await.map_err(|error| DbErr::Custom(error.to_string()))?; After each commit, an instance tells the others (NOTIFY on the channel cqrs_events, after the commit and from a connection of its own, so the appends never wait on it); each instance LISTENs and wakes its readers, which then read the store at once. Keep the returned Listening: dropping it stops the relay. A lost notification only costs the poll's latency; the store stays the source of truth. Subscriptions across instances. Every instance runs an emitter per namespace with an updated: it follows the committed events and emits once the namespace handled each one, whichever instance did. A client subscribed to any instance gets every change, as soon as the relay above wakes it. Rebuilding the read model. Stop every instance, then reset the projection: each namespace's tokens go back to the start, then its reset runs in a transaction (for summaries, clear). On the next start, summaries replays the whole log; notifications (REPLAY = false) skips what it already handled. A reset refuses to run while an instance still holds a segment. pg.events::<PostEvent>("posts") .projection(PostProjection::new(summaries, notifier)) .reset() .await?; Failing events. A failing event rolls its unit of work back and is retried with growing waits (retry_initial, retry_max), holding back the later events of its segment; the processor's status().failing reports the error. A projection can park such events instead, in PostgresDeadLetters: .projection_with(projection, |processors| processors.with_dead_letters(PostgresDeadLetters::new(pg.store("posts")), n)) on the builder, and the same for a processor built by hand (Event processing § Dead letters). Changing an event's shape. Bump its version and give the store an upcaster: pg.store::<PostEvent>("posts").with_upcasters(upcast("post.created", 1, |payload| ..)), then build the Events by hand as above (Storage § Upcasting). Next: 9. The API.

A projection turns committed events into read models and side effects. There is one per aggregate root: a struct holding what its handlers need, with one event handler per namespace. Each namespace is run on its own, with its own position in the log, so a failing notification never holds the read model back.

// src/application/projections/post/mod.rs #[cqrs::projection( name = "post", events = PostEvent, namespaces("summaries", "notifications"), updates(FindPost, ListPublished), subscriptions = PostSubscriptions )] pub struct PostProjection<S, N> { /// Where the summaries are kept. summaries: Arc<S>, /// Who delivers the announcements. notifier: Arc<N>, } impl<S, N> PostProjection<S, N> { pub fn new(summaries: Arc<S>, notifier: Arc<N>) -> Self { Self { summaries, notifier } } } name and namespaces(..) name the processors that will run it, one per namespace: "post.summaries" and "post.notifications". Each keys its own tokens (Axon's @Namespace). events = PostEvent: a projection follows one aggregate's events. The namespace lives on the projection, not on the event: the domain does not know who consumes it. updates(..) and subscriptions = .. are for subscription queries (part 6). The compiler checks both ways: a namespace listed without its handler cannot run, and a handler for a namespace not listed does not compile. Each namespace gets a file of its own: src/application/projections/ ├── mod.rs └── post/ ├── mod.rs # PostProjection ├── summaries.rs # the read model └── notifications.rs # a side effect

// src/application/projections/post/summaries.rs use cqrs::{ event::EventEnvelope, processing::{EventHandler, HandlerError, ProcessingContext}, }; #[cqrs::event_handler(namespace = "summaries", batch = 64)] impl<S, N, Tx> EventHandler for PostProjection<S, N> where S: PostSummaryRepository + PostSummaryStore<Tx>, N: Send + Sync, Tx: Send, { async fn handle( &self, event: &EventEnvelope<PostEvent>, context: &mut ProcessingContext<'_, Tx>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerError> { let tx = context.transaction(); let found = match &event.payload { PostEvent::Created { id, title } => { let summary = PostSummary { id: *id, title: title.clone(), published: false, }; self.summaries.save(tx, summary).await?; true } PostEvent::Retitled { title } => { self.summaries .update(tx, post_of(event)?, |s| s.title.clone_from(title)) .await? } PostEvent::Published => { self.summaries .update(tx, post_of(event)?, |s| s.published = true) .await? } }; if !found { // Events of a stream arrive in order, its creation first. return Err(HandlerError::msg(format!( "{} has no summary: its creation was not projected", event.stream ))); } Ok(()) } /// Before a replay rebuilds it. async fn reset(&self, context: &mut ProcessingContext<'_, Tx>) -> Result<(), HandlerError> { self.summaries.clear(context.transaction()).await?; Ok(()) } // `updated`, which pushes the new summaries to subscribers: part 6. } /// The post an event belongs to. fn post_of(event: &EventEnvelope<PostEvent>) -> Result<PostId, HandlerError> { event .aggregate_id::<Post>() .ok_or_else(|| HandlerError::msg(format!("not a post stream: {}", event.stream))) } The envelope carries the event (payload) and what the store recorded about it: stream, sequence, position, recorded_at, metadata. aggregate_id::<Post>() reads the post's id back from the stream. What #[cqrs::event_handler(namespace = "summaries", batch = 64)] does: reads the event type from &EventEnvelope<PostEvent> and the unit of work from &mut ProcessingContext<'_, Tx>; makes the impl the handler of the summaries namespace; batch = 64: up to 64 waiting events are handled in one unit of work, with one token update. The default is 1, as in Axon. The unit of work is a type parameter. The handler writes through PostSummaryStore<Tx>, the write half of the read model's port (part 3), in the transaction the processor hands it (context.transaction()). In memory Tx is (); on PostgreSQL it is the processor's transaction, so each change commits with the processor's token (part 8). The projection does not choose: the composition root does, by picking the adapter. Why a batch. Everything this handler does is undone with its transaction, so batching is safe: a failing batch is rolled back and its events handled again one at a time. Rebuilding 5000 events took 0.25 s with batches of 64, instead of 4.6 s one by one. Things the projection does not do: Check sequences or remember what it applied. Whoever runs it delivers each post's events once and in order (part 5 shows how a processor guarantees it with its unit of work). Read the event store. Everything it needs is in the event.

The application declares the port it needs, next to the handler that uses it: // src/application/projections/post/notifications.rs /// Port to whatever delivers notifications (e-mail, chat, ...). pub trait Notifier: Send + Sync { fn notify(&self, message: String) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), NotificationError>> + Send; } /// Announces every post that gets published. A notification already went /// out: a replay must not send it again, so it does not see replays; and /// it is not undone with a transaction, so it takes events one at a time /// (no `batch`): a failing batch, handled again, would send it twice. #[cqrs::event_handler(namespace = "notifications")] impl<S: Send + Sync, N: Notifier> EventHandler for PostProjection<S, N> { const REPLAY: bool = false; async fn handle( &self, event: &EventEnvelope<PostEvent>, _: &mut ProcessingContext<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerError> { if let PostEvent::Published = event.payload { self.notifier.notify(format!("{} published", event.stream)).await?; } Ok(()) } } To the library, a side effect is just another namespace. Two settings make the difference: REPLAY = false: when the projection is replayed (part 5), the summaries are rebuilt, but nobody is notified again. No batch: a notification cannot be rolled back, so a failed batch handled again would send some twice. Its context names no Tx, so it runs in any unit of work. This is also where side effects of a command go. A command handler is run again when it loses a race for the post (part 2), so it must not send anything itself: it records events, and a namespace reacts to them once they are committed. InMemoryNotifier (infrastructure) records the messages and can be switched off to simulate an outage.

All the wiring lives in one file, src/config.rs, the only one that names concrete adapters. It creates the stores and the services, and builds the blog's CQRS unit with a typed builder: // src/config.rs pub type PostStore = InMemoryEventStore<PostEvent>; pub fn in_memory_with( store: PostStore, ) -> ( Cqrs<impl PostCommands, impl PostQueries>, Arc<InMemoryPostSummaryRepository>, Arc<InMemoryNotifier>, ) { let summaries = Arc::new(InMemoryPostSummaryRepository::default()); let notifier = Arc::new(InMemoryNotifier::default()); // Synchronous: no subscriptions to push updates to. Each namespace runs // isolated: a failing notification never holds the read model back. let projection = PostProjection::new(Arc::clone(&summaries), Arc::clone(&notifier)); let publisher = InlinePublisher::<PostEvent, _, _>::new(store.clone()).with_projection(projection); let blog = Cqrs::from_publisher(publisher) .commands(|events| PostCommandGateway::new(posts_over(&store), events)) .queries(PostQueryGateway::new(Arc::clone(&summaries))) .build(); (blog, summaries, notifier) } in_memory() is in_memory_with(PostStore::default()); posts_over(&store) is the event-sourced repository from part 2, over the same store. The store is created here and shared: the repository reads it, the publisher writes it. The publisher is an InlinePublisher over the store. With with_projection, it runs every namespace right after each commit, in the caller's task, no runtime needed. It is built by hand (Cqrs::from_publisher) because it runs the handlers inline; part 5 starts from Cqrs::new(Events::new(store)) instead. .commands(|events| ..) hands the closure the unit's publisher, which the command gateway keeps as its #[gateway(unit)] field: the unit of work every command commits through. The query gateway needs none. Each step changes the builder's type, so the order is checked, and every type is inferred. What the unit exposes is named by the traits the gateways generate: impl PostCommands, impl PostQueries. The unit has commands(), queries() and events().

// tests/flow.rs use blog::{application::{commands::*, queries::*}, in_memory}; use cqrs::{command::CommandGateway, query::QueryGateway, testing::block_on}; #[test] fn a_command_commits_events_and_the_projection_answers_queries() { block_on(async { let (blog, _, notifier) = in_memory(); let id = blog.commands().send(CreatePost { title: "Static dispatch".into() }).await.unwrap(); blog.commands().send(PublishPost { id }).await.unwrap(); let found = blog.queries().query(FindPost { id }).await.unwrap(); assert_eq!(found, Some(PostSummary { id, title: "Static dispatch".into(), published: true })); assert_eq!(blog.queries().query(ListPublished).await.unwrap().len(), 1); assert_eq!(notifier.sent(), ["post-1 published"]); }); } Inline, a failing handler never undoes the commit, and does not stop the other namespace. The publisher logs the failure (or hands it to what you give InlinePublisher::on_failure(|failure| ..)), and the command still succeeds: notifier.set_down(true); blog.commands().send(PublishPost { id }).await.unwrap(); // the notification failed (logged)... assert!(summaries.find(id).await.unwrap().unwrap().published); // ...but the event is stored and the summary updated Inline processing has no retries, no positions and no replays: fine for tests and small tools. Part 5 moves the namespaces to tracking processors. A projection is also easy to test alone, by replaying events into one of its namespaces (summaries is index 0, in the order namespaces(..) lists them): // tests/flow.rs use cqrs::processing::{ProcessingContext, Route}; let projection = PostProjection::new(Arc::clone(&summaries), Arc::new(InMemoryNotifier::default())); projection.reset(0, &mut ProcessingContext::new(&mut (), false)).await.unwrap(); for event in store.all() { // the store `in_memory_with(store)` was given projection.handle(0, &event, &mut ProcessingContext::new(&mut (), true)).await.unwrap(); } assert_eq!(summaries.find(id).await.unwrap().unwrap().title, "b"); Next: 5. Going asynchronous.

Queries never read the event store. They read a read model, a shape made for the screens that need it, kept up to date from the events by a projection (part 4). Here we define the read model, the ports it is kept behind, the queries and their gateway.

// src/application/queries/post_summary.rs use std::future::Future; use cqrs::store::StoreError; use crate::domain::PostId; /// A post as the read side shows it. #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] pub struct PostSummary { pub id: PostId, pub title: String, pub published: bool, } /// The read model, as the queries read it. It is fed by committed events, /// so it is eventually consistent with the write side. pub trait PostSummaryRepository: Send + Sync { /// The summary of one post, or `None` if the read model has not seen it /// (it may not exist, or its creation may not be projected yet). fn find(&self, id: PostId) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Option<PostSummary>, StoreError>> + Send; /// Published posts, ordered by id. fn published(&self) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Vec<PostSummary>, StoreError>> + Send; } /// The read model, as the projection writes it: in the unit of work `Tx` /// the processor hands it with each event, so a read model in the same /// database as the processor's tokens commits each change with its token /// (an event is applied once). In memory, `Tx` is `()`. pub trait PostSummaryStore<Tx>: Send + Sync { /// Stores a new post's `summary`. fn save(&self, tx: &mut Tx, summary: PostSummary) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), StoreError>> + Send; /// Changes the summary of `id` with `change`; `false` if there is none. fn update( &self, tx: &mut Tx, id: PostId, change: impl FnOnce(&mut PostSummary) + Send, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<bool, StoreError>> + Send; /// Removes every summary, before a replay rebuilds them. fn clear(&self, tx: &mut Tx) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), StoreError>> + Send; } The ports are in the application layer: what the read side needs is application logic; where it lives is an adapter's business. Why this shape: Two ports, two callers. Queries only read, outside any transaction. The projection only writes, in the unit of work of the processor that runs it (part 4): on PostgreSQL, that is the transaction that also saves the processor's progress, so a change and its token commit together (part 8). Not the write side's repository. PostRepository finds an aggregate to decide on; this one stores rows shaped for reading. They differ in storage, consistency and callers, so they stay different types. update takes a closure (Axon's managed entity): the adapter applies the change in place, so a projection never does find, clone, save.
documents.s: The read model and its ports

documents.t: // src/infrastructure/post_summary_repository.rs use std::{collections::BTreeMap, sync::Mutex}; use cqrs::store::StoreError; /// The read model in memory: one row per post. Its unit of work is `()`: /// there is nothing to roll back. #[derive(Default)] pub struct InMemoryPostSummaryRepository { /// Rows by id (so listings come out sorted). rows: Mutex<BTreeMap<PostId, PostSummary>>, } impl PostSummaryRepository for InMemoryPostSummaryRepository { async fn find(&self, id: PostId) -> Result<Option<PostSummary>, StoreError> { Ok(self.rows().get(&id).cloned()) } async fn published(&self) -> Result<Vec<PostSummary>, StoreError> { Ok(self.rows().values().filter(|summary| summary.published).cloned().collect()) } } impl PostSummaryStore<()> for InMemoryPostSummaryRepository { async fn save(&self, (): &mut (), summary: PostSummary) -> Result<(), StoreError> { self.rows().insert(summary.id, summary); Ok(()) } async fn update( &self, (): &mut (), id: PostId, change: impl FnOnce(&mut PostSummary) + Send, ) -> Result<bool, StoreError> { Ok(self.rows().get_mut(&id).map(change).is_some()) } async fn clear(&self, (): &mut ()) -> Result<(), StoreError> { self.rows().clear(); Ok(()) } } (rows() locks the map.) On PostgreSQL, SeaOrmPostSummaries implements the same two ports (part 8).

// src/application/queries/mod.rs #[cqrs::query_gateway(queries = PostQueries, handles(FindPost, ListPublished))] pub struct PostQueryGateway<M> { /// The read model, shared with the projection that writes it. summaries: Arc<M>, } impl<M> PostQueryGateway<M> { pub fn new(summaries: Arc<M>) -> Self { Self { summaries } } } The query counterpart of the command gateway (part 2): the gateway is the handler, with one QueryHandler<Q> impl per query, sharing the read model. A query listed in handles(..) without its impl does not compile. There is no unit of work: a query writes nothing. queries = PostQueries generates the trait QueryGateway<FindPost> + QueryGateway<ListPublished>, implemented by whatever answers both. Subscribing to the queries is a different trait, PostSubscriptions, generated by the projection that pushes their updates (part 6).

// src/application/queries/find_post.rs use cqrs::query::QueryHandler; use super::{PostQueryGateway, PostSummary, PostSummaryRepository}; use crate::{application::BlogError, domain::PostId}; /// One post, published or not; `None` if it does not exist (yet). #[cqrs::query(output = Option<PostSummary>, error = BlogError)] #[derive(Clone, Debug)] pub struct FindPost { pub id: PostId, } /// Answers from the read model. #[cqrs::query_handler] impl<M: PostSummaryRepository> QueryHandler<FindPost> for PostQueryGateway<M> { async fn handle(&self, query: FindPost) -> Result<Option<PostSummary>, BlogError> { Ok(self.summaries.find(query.id).await?) } } // src/application/queries/list_published.rs /// Every published post, ordered by id. #[cqrs::query(output = Vec<PostSummary>, error = BlogError)] #[derive(Clone, Debug)] pub struct ListPublished; #[cqrs::query_handler] impl<M: PostSummaryRepository> QueryHandler<ListPublished> for PostQueryGateway<M> { async fn handle(&self, _: ListPublished) -> Result<Vec<PostSummary>, BlogError> { Ok(self.summaries.published().await?) } } #[cqrs::query(output = T, error = E)] makes the struct a Query. A query and a command are different marker traits, so a query can never be sent as a command, or the other way around: a compile error. The handler bounds only what it uses (M: PostSummaryRepository), never the projection's PostSummaryStore: a query cannot write. The query is taken by value: queries are never rerun. #[cqrs::query_handler] marks the gateway as answering the query, for handles(..) (and fills in Q if the impl leaves it out). Asking is query: let found: Option<PostSummary> = gateway.query(FindPost { id }).await?; At this point commands store events and queries read summaries, but nothing writes the summaries. That is the projection. Next: 4. The projection.
